intro.h: In Rockfon sales, a good result depends on more than a convincing product presentation. A salesperson needs to understand the project, recognise who influences the decision, explore the requirements, and agree useful next steps. They also need to work effectively with architects, consultants, contractors, installers, distributors and colleagues as the project develops.

A manager can help with an immediate issue by providing an answer. Coaching also helps the person handle the next issue with more confidence and independence. That development matters when the manager cannot attend every meeting or make every project decision.

Coaching is a structured conversation that helps someone understand a situation, examine their thinking, choose an appropriate action and take responsibility for it. The manager listens, asks questions, provides support and follows up. The salesperson contributes their experience, does the thinking and carries out the agreed work.

Coaching can help with three linked kinds of problem: skills, such as asking useful questions; working methods, such as a consistent project follow-up routine; and thinking, such as assuming that another contact will annoy a customer. Similar activities can produce different results when the person's understanding, confidence or execution differs. Project conditions and available resources also matter.

The aim is to improve decisions and performance while developing people. Keep the work requirement clear, and remain open to what the person needs to meet it. A useful conversation may reveal a different problem from the one the manager expected.

blocks.h: The manager has six connected responsibilities:

items: Use strengths. Identify capabilities the person can build on, rather than describing them only through shortcomings.
Make progress easier. Help remove confusion, obstacles and missing resources.
Develop capability. Help the person use their strengths more effectively and improve the skills needed for the role.
Request growth. Ask for a meaningful improvement and provide guidance where necessary.
Ask useful questions. Help the person think clearly rather than expecting the manager to have every answer.
Build accountability. Make ownership of actions, results and learning explicit.

blocks.h: During a coaching conversation:

items: Explore the interests and motivations that make the work meaningful to the person.
Identify natural strengths, skills and experience that can help.
Clarify the person's professional goals and relevant personal priorities they choose to discuss.
Develop options and an achievable action plan together.
Provide guidance, structure, resources, encouragement and practical support.
Create a respectful environment in which difficulties can be discussed honestly.
Challenge assumptions or habits that may be limiting performance.
Build progress through focused action and reliable follow-up.

blocks.h: Accountability means agreeing what will be done, who will do it and how progress will be reviewed. It includes recognising results, discussing missed commitments and learning from what happened. The relationship supports the person; it does not remove the responsibility to address work that falls short of agreed standards.

sections.title: Choose the right kind of support

intro.h: Not every development need is a coaching need. A person who has never learned a task may need instruction before questions become useful. Someone who knows the method but struggles to apply it may benefit from coaching. A commercial or technical issue may require advice or specialist input.

head: Contribution
What it provides
When it helps
rows: Coaching
Questions, reflection, practical support and accountability
The person has a foundation and needs to improve their thinking, decisions or execution
Training
Explanation, demonstration and practice
The person needs to learn a skill or working method
Mentoring
Guidance from relevant experience
The person needs perspective on a role, career or familiar business situation
Consulting or specialist advice
Analysis, recommendations or expert information
A decision depends on knowledge or analysis the person does not yet have

intro.h: Choose the contribution that addresses the actual gap. These forms of support can be combined. For example, a salesperson may need technical guidance to understand a ceiling-system requirement, practice to explain it clearly, and coaching to prepare questions for a project meeting.

Learning can take different forms: preparation exercises or assessments; role-play; practice scenarios; individual instruction; small-group discussions; interactive questions, panels or forums; scripts, templates and technical material; and joint exercises that produce a usable output. Match the activity to what the person needs to do differently.
Do not keep asking questions when a person needs a clear explanation or a management decision. Equally, do not turn every request for help into a demonstration of the manager's expertise.

subs.title: Five practices of an effective coach

items: Understand the work. Relevant sales and leadership experience helps you recognise the demands of the role and provide useful guidance. Check the current situation rather than assuming it matches your own experience.
Model the expected behaviour. Your preparation, customer communication, work habits and follow-through show what the standard looks like in practice.
Provide an answer when it is needed. Advice, instruction or specialist support can remove an unnecessary barrier. Explain enough for the person to understand and use the answer.
Pay attention to the person. A conversation plan can help, but it should not prevent you from hearing an unexpected concern or asking a more useful question.
Develop a natural coaching style. Use methods that fit your strengths and values. Consistent practice is more useful than trying to sound like someone else.

blocks.h: Effective coaching combines confidence with humility. Give people enough time, check that your message was understood, share useful expertise and put their development ahead of protecting your own image. Technical knowledge and people-development skills both need attention.

subs.title: Six failure modes and one approach to develop

blocks.h: The first six patterns are failure modes: unproductive habits to recognise and correct. They are not roles to aim for. Each begins with a useful strength that becomes costly when it is overused or applied badly. Any manager can fall into several patterns, especially under pressure.

head: Pattern
Useful strength
Unproductive weakness
A more useful response
rows: Hero — failure mode
Willingness to help and find solutions
Takes over the thinking and work, creating dependence
Ask for the person's diagnosis and options; provide the support they need to act
Pressuring — failure mode
Persistence, directness and willingness to address performance
Relies on threats or constant pushing
Connect the work to a meaningful goal and agree clear accountability
Talk A Lot — failure mode
Energy, enthusiasm and ability to engage people
Speaks before understanding and gives too little attention to listening or follow-up
Listen, clarify the real need, and agree an action and review
Know it Best — failure mode
Confidence and decisiveness
Treats assumptions as facts, or protects personal methods, results or status
Check evidence, consider another perspective and share expertise
Need to be Perfect — failure mode
Knowledge, organisation, efficiency and commitment to improvement
Overcontrols work, overloads people with information, or delays action in search of a perfect method

Avoids difficult feedback or expectations to preserve comfort or approval

blocks.h: The Proactive approach uses the valuable qualities of the other patterns without keeping their unproductive habits. Notice a behaviour and its effect. Do not turn the name into a permanent label for yourself or a colleague.

intro.h: A manager's assumptions can shape a conversation before the salesperson has explained the situation. Under pressure, it is easy to listen mainly for agreement, defend a familiar solution or protect a preferred result. These habits can prevent a useful diagnosis.

blocks.h: Watch for a strong need to:

items: Be right or appear capable.
Obtain a particular result from the conversation.
Be understood or prove a point.
Secure agreement.
Avoid being wrong, looking unprepared or hearing “no”.

blocks.h: Repeating the same argument or trying harder to make someone accept your view can be a sign that one of these needs is taking over. The costs can include:

items: Missing a better solution.
Blocking useful contributions because you are not listening fully.
Dismissing the person's feelings or perspective.
Failing to adjust your communication to the person.
Losing flexibility when new information appears.
Missing the issue that coaching could usefully address.

blocks.h: Keep the required standard clear while allowing flexibility in how it is met. A goal gives direction. It does not prove that the manager's first solution is the best way forward. Before responding, ask yourself: “What am I trying to protect, and what have I not yet understood?”

When a project stalls, people can quickly accept an explanation as fact: “The contractor only cares about price,” or “The architect will not consider a change.” The explanation may be correct, partly correct or wrong. Coaching helps separate what is known from what has been inferred.
Pay attention to five elements of the person's account:

items: The story: the explanation built around what happened.
The justification: the reason used to defend a behaviour or avoid a difficult action.
The assumption: something treated as true without enough confirmation.
The meaning: what the event is taken to say about the person, customer or situation.
The mindset: a repeated way of thinking that shapes expectations and action.

blocks.h: These elements can appear as:

items: An explanation for behaviour that is not helping.
Action, inaction or a belief that avoids responsibility.
A recurring complaint without a changed response.
Repeated blame, urgency, conflict or perfectionism that absorbs attention.
A justification for circumstances in the past, present or expected future.
A past experience treated as a fixed explanation of who someone is.
A reason for continuing behaviour that conflicts with a stated goal.

blocks.h: Start with the evidence. Ask what was actually said or done, what the person concluded, and what remains uncertain. Explore another interpretation only when it is plausible. Then agree how to test it through a question, observation or action. A different interpretation does not remove a real workload problem, resource shortage or customer requirement.

subs.title: Ten thinking habits to notice in ourselves

blocks.h: Use these as possibilities to examine, not as diagnoses of a colleague.

items: Avoiding a possible failure. Delaying action reduces immediate discomfort but also removes the opportunity to learn or succeed.
Waiting for a perfect approach. More preparation becomes a substitute for trying a reasonable method and improving it.
Keeping too much work. Assuming nobody else can do it well enough prevents delegation and development.
Generalising from one attempt. A previous disappointment is treated as proof that an approach can never work.
Staying with familiar activity. Looking after existing contacts replaces the less comfortable work of creating new opportunities.
Making commitments without a completion point. A task is listed but has no date or protected time.
Working without a routine. Constant busyness becomes the reason not to plan the work.
Agreeing to too much. Other people's requests repeatedly displace existing commitments.
Allowing interruptions to lead the day. Urgent requests and unfinished work become a familiar pattern that goes unexamined.
Letting a setback shape the next response. One difficult event is allowed to determine the rest of the day.

blocks.h: Describe the behaviour, its effect and a possible alternative. Ask what would make a different action realistic. Some barriers require a change in resources or workload as well as a change in thinking.

subs.title: Assess performance without imposing your own preferences

blocks.h: Managers need to judge whether work meets requirements. That is different from assuming that a salesperson should share the manager's goals, selling style or personal definition of success.
Before concluding, check whether you are assuming that the person:

items: Should be further ahead in their development.
Should want a higher goal.
Should already have secured a particular project.
Should always feel positive about work.
Should already know how to do something.
Must know the technical detail because of their length of service.
Should handle a conversation exactly as you would.
Must make more outbound contacts regardless of the quality or purpose of the activity.
Must be underperforming for a reason that the sales figures alone can explain.

blocks.h: Observe the work and discuss the evidence. A sustained performance gap may require a clear management decision. During a development conversation, understand the person's goals and needs while maintaining the requirements of the role.

subs.title: Keep attention on the person's development

blocks.h: It is natural for a manager to worry about saying the wrong thing, looking unprepared, pushing too hard, being rejected, being seen as unfair or failing. Other pressures include needing the salesperson to succeed, wanting to prove your value, wanting to avoid another recruitment process, or needing results for your own targets.

Notice these ten pressures without allowing them to determine the conversation. Ask: “What would help this person understand the issue and act more effectively?” If you find yourself repeatedly pushing for agreement, check whether your own concern has replaced their development need.

intro.h: Coaching time is limited. Use it where a meaningful development need and a willingness to act are present. People who already perform well also need development; repeated emergencies should not automatically absorb all available attention.

Do not continue the same coaching conversation indefinitely when agreed actions are repeatedly avoided. First investigate the barrier. Missing skill calls for training, missing resources call for support, and unclear expectations call for clarification. Continued unwillingness to meet a clear work requirement needs to be addressed directly.

blocks.h: Coachability means being ready and able to benefit from coaching. It is something to explore with the person, not a label based on how quickly they agree with the manager.

items: Ability to act. Can the person carry out the work, and will they try the actions needed? Capability without action and effort without the necessary skill each need a different response.
A meaningful gap. Is there a clear difference between present and desired performance that development can help address?
Responsibility and ownership. Will the person examine their contribution, keep commitments and take responsibility for the next action?
Willingness. Do their actions show commitment to the goal, including when the work becomes difficult?
Trust. Is there enough confidence in the relationship for coaching to be useful? If not, understand what damaged it and whether it can be rebuilt.
Honesty. Can the person discuss relevant difficulties and consider information they may not want to hear? Trust and honesty are connected, but they are not the same condition.

blocks.h: These are discussion and decision criteria, not a scored assessment or a pass mark. Check readiness through what the person actually does. A concern about the process, a resource limitation or a different view is not automatically a lack of coachability.

subs.title: Understand the gap before choosing the response

blocks.h: The development gap is the difference between the current situation and the outcome the person wants or needs to achieve. Describe both clearly before deciding what to do.
Examine four dimensions:

items: Knowledge and understanding: what the person knows, believes or assumes compared with what they need to understand.
Activity: what they currently do compared with the actions needed to support the goal.
Resources, skills and methods: what is available and what is missing.
Results: what is happening compared with the intended outcome.

blocks.h: Ask the person to describe a recent, specific situation. Where possible, observe a conversation, meeting preparation or follow-up action. Establish the sequence, the language used, the customer's response and the agreed next step. General statements such as “I always follow up” are less useful than a concrete account.

Then decide what support fits. Demonstrate an unfamiliar task. Provide missing information or specialist input. Use coaching where the person can think through the issue but needs to examine a choice, assumption or habit. Several gaps may exist together. A weak follow-up routine, uncertainty about the next project decision and fear of bothering the customer may all need attention.

subs.title: Ten areas that coaching can address

items: The person: values, interests, standards, boundaries and the qualities they want to bring to work.
Attitude and thinking: beliefs, assumptions, expectations and ways of interpreting events.
Learning: what experience has taught them and whether that learning changes their actions.
Professional qualities: relevant expectations such as honesty, communication, curiosity, preparation and reliability.
Skills: capabilities that need to be learned or improved.
Activity: whether daily actions support the goal.
Strategy: the intended approach, its sequence and the resources required.
Commitment: consistency, effort and follow-through.
Communication: wording, questions, tone, listening and how the message is received.
Relationships: working relationships and the person's response to concerns, beliefs and recurring explanations.

blocks.h: Choose an area because it helps explain an observed gap. Do not turn the list into ten questions to ask at every meeting.

Lars - a new salesperson preparing for an architect meeting. Lars has not yet learned how to explore a project's acoustic-ceiling requirements. Asking him to invent a complete approach would add confusion. Demonstrate the preparation and questioning method, explain the relevant technical information and practise the conversation. Coaching can then help him review what happened and improve the next meeting.

Maria - an experienced salesperson with a narrow project pipeline. Maria has relied on a few strong relationships, and several projects are now delayed. She is active but does not have a consistent method for identifying and qualifying new opportunities. Help her define a repeatable contact approach, document the sequence, obtain suitable prospect and project information, and practise the language. Coach the worry behind her choices as well as the working method. Agree what evidence will show useful new conversations, not just activity.

Tom - good project access, weak progress after presentations. Tom secures meetings but sends extensive product information without finding out what the customer needs to decide. Explore what he believes a presentation should achieve and whether he is avoiding questions or a request for a next step. Practise handling concerns and asking for a clear commitment. Help him check the project fit and decision process rather than assuming that more information will create progress.
These are illustrative situations for practice. They do not describe actual employees or reported Rockfon results.

intro.h: Talking too much or assuming you already understand can make a conversation sound helpful while leaving the actual issue untouched. Listening is an active task: pay attention, try to understand what is meant, and check your understanding before you choose a response.

items: Doing another task or thinking about something else.
Only waiting for a gap to make your own point, instead of listening.
Speaking automatically instead of allowing a quiet moment to think.
Pretending to listen while you wait for your turn to speak.
Hearing only the information that fits your expectations.
Missing relevant tone, facial expression, gestures or other nonverbal information.
Allowing noise, notifications or other distractions to interfere.
Listening through assumptions formed by past experience, expected results or judgements about the speaker.

blocks.h: Filters can be positive as well as negative. Respect for an experienced colleague can make you accept an explanation too easily; frustration after a previous missed commitment can make you stop hearing new evidence. Accent, status, appearance and age do not establish the value of someone's message.

Separate facts from interpretation. Ask whether the customer actually stated a concern or whether the salesperson inferred it. “They rejected the proposal” may mean “They asked for further information.” Both deserve attention, but they require different responses.

Allow a pause. A pause of about three to five seconds can help both people think. It can create room to explore an issue, process information, build trust, share more and avoid an immediate defensive reply. Use silence naturally; do not turn it into a timing rule for every response.

Attend to the message. Give the person your attention without allowing their status or style to determine what you hear. A telephone conversation can reduce visual distractions; a face-to-face conversation also offers useful nonverbal information. In either case, verify your interpretation.

items: The underlying need. A request for more leads may reflect weak qualification. A request for more time may reflect an unclear routine. Explore the need before accepting the first proposed solution.
What matters to the person. Listen for priorities, goals, the work experience they want and the support they expect from you.
Facts and assumptions. Notice where evidence ends and explanation begins.
Concerns and fears. Make room for worries about the customer, products, service, colleagues, the working method or the manager.
The development gap. Identify missing skill, information, resources, strategy, ownership or understanding.

blocks.h: Listening for these areas does not mean guessing what someone is hiding. Treat an impression as a question to check. A request for more product training might show a need to practise asking about the customer's decision criteria, not a lack of technical knowledge.

subs.title: Check understanding and show that you have heard

blocks.h: Restate the meaning in your own words and ask whether you understood correctly. This both checks accuracy and shows that the person's contribution matters.
Useful ways to clarify include:

items: Check an interpretation: “Have I understood you correctly?”
Summarise the central issue: “It sounds as though the main concern is…”
Reflect what you heard: “You said the project timing changed. Is that right?”
Ask for help understanding: “Can you help me understand that?”
Ask for an explanation: “What do you mean by that?”
Invite detail: “Can you tell me more?”
Check decision criteria: “What are you using to decide?”
Clarify action: “What happens next?”
Review the discussion: “Let me check the main points so far.”
Clarify an unclear word: “What does ‘confirmed’ mean in this situation?”
Invite different wording: “Could you explain that another way?”

blocks.h: Restating and checking can improve shared understanding, stimulate thinking and help the person continue the conversation. It can also build credibility, strengthen the relationship and encourage both people to listen. Checking reduces premature judgement, unsolicited solutions and responses driven by assumptions. A confident summary that is never checked can still be wrong.

intro.h: The Hero habit is attractive when a decision feels urgent: the manager gives an answer and work moves forward. Repeated too often, it teaches the salesperson to bring the next problem back to the manager. A quick answer can create long-term dependence.

subs.title: Let the salesperson do the thinking

blocks.h: Aim to develop four outcomes: continued improvement; people solving their own challenges; future leaders; and motivation that does not depend on constant pushing from the manager.

Six common reasons for taking over are habit, believing the boss should have every answer, copying a previous manager, feeling useful when solving problems, postponing coaching until work is quieter, and assuming an answer is always the fastest option. Notice which applies before you respond.

Ask the person to describe the issue, offer their view of the cause and suggest options. Identify missing knowledge, skill, resources or process. Provide what is needed, then ask them to choose and explain the next action. The salesperson owns the thinking and work; the manager remains responsible for suitable instruction and support.

For example: “What decision needs to move forward on this project? What do we know about who influences it? Which next contact would you choose, and why?” If the salesperson does not know how to map the decision process, teach that method before expecting an independent answer.

items: Increase awareness by examining perceptions, assumptions and behaviour.
Build ownership by helping the person develop a solution they understand and can use.
Reduce unnecessary pressure and make a more constructive relationship possible.
Clarify thinking about needs, goals, concerns, values and opinions.
Help people discover the facts rather than simply accepting the manager's conclusion.
Improve the manager's listening by creating a reason to investigate rather than speak.
Build commitment through choice and understanding rather than relying only on instructions.

blocks.h: A question is useful because of its purpose and effect, not because it ends with a question mark. Tone, timing and the manager's agenda can turn it into an accusation or a way to force a preferred answer. Ask one clear question, allow a response and use what you hear.

subs.title: Move from blame to a workable next step

head: A question that can trigger defensiveness
A more useful direction
rows: “What is wrong with you?”
“What can we learn? What worked, and what could you handle differently?”
“Why do you keep failing?”
“What needs to change, and what would help you get it right next time?”
“Why was this not done correctly?”
“Which action, skill, tool or resource was missing?”
“Why can you never update the project record on time?”
“What routine would make the update reliable, and what support do you need?”
“Why does this happen in every customer meeting?”
“Where does the conversation become difficult, and what could prevent that?”
“Why are you always late?”
“What needs to change so you can meet the agreed time consistently?”

blocks.h: “Why” is not a prohibited word. Asking why a goal matters can be valuable. The issue is whether the question helps understanding and action or mainly asks the person to defend themselves.

intro.h: Persistence is useful. Constant pressure is costly. If people act mainly to avoid a threat, the manager often has to keep up the pressure. A more sustainable approach connects clear work requirements with an outcome the person values.

blocks.h: Push means moving someone away from a feared loss through pressure, threats or repeated warnings. It relies heavily on the manager to maintain activity.

Pull means helping the person move towards a meaningful goal, supported by a clear plan and accountability. It aims to build commitment within the person rather than requiring the manager to create all the energy.

Find out what matters to the individual. Money may matter, but so may competence, recognition, flexibility, stability, development or the satisfaction of helping a project succeed. Delegation can also motivate when it communicates trust and gives the person real ownership.
Common standards can coexist with different needs and selling styles. Do not assume that one incentive, phrase or reward will work equally well for everyone.

subs.title: Ten questions about motivation and preferred support

blocks.h: Use an individual conversation. Ask naturally, listen and follow up on what the person says.

items: What would you like to do more of, and what would make your work more engaging?
Which capabilities would you like to develop?
What matters most to you in work and life, and what does success mean to you?
Which three achievements would give you the greatest satisfaction now?
What is your plan for achieving them?
What could prevent progress?
How can I support you best?
How would you like me to help you stay accountable for the results you want?
What would make accountability feel useful rather than controlling?
If you miss a commitment, how should I raise it so that we can discuss it openly?

blocks.h: Agree what support and accountability will look like. Where a requirement is fixed, explain it clearly rather than presenting it as an optional personal goal.

subs.title: Connect effort to a meaningful outcome

blocks.h: Describe the benefit of completing the work. A consistent project follow-up routine can help a salesperson prepare better conversations, reduce last-minute requests and understand which projects need attention. A learning goal can make a difficult meeting easier to handle. A well-planned handover can reduce unfinished work before leave.

Consequences also matter. Ask what continued inaction could cost the project, customer, salesperson or team. Help the person understand that cost without making fear the normal way of managing people. A transparent discussion of an agreed consequence is different from repeated threats.

Some managers hold back recognition. They may not know how to give it, may fear it will reduce effort, may think it is unimportant or may worry that it will sound insincere. Specific recognition makes clear what is worth repeating.
Name the action, its useful effect and your appreciation. Acknowledge an achievement on its own merits; do not immediately spoil it with unrelated criticism or an administrative reminder.
Illustrative examples:

items: “You checked the contractor's concern and agreed a useful next step instead of sending another general presentation. That made the follow-up more relevant. Thank you for adapting your approach.”
“You delivered the project proposal when agreed, despite several competing deadlines. Your planning helped the team meet its commitment.”
“You involved technical support and the distributor early rather than carrying the issue alone. That gave everyone time to prepare and kept responsibilities clear.”

blocks.h: Recognise effort, improvement and sound working habits as well as the final order. Be accurate about what you observed; do not claim a result that has not happened.

intro.h: People are more able to examine an issue when the manager respects their effort and treats them as capable of learning. Respect does not require agreement that inaccurate information or incomplete work is acceptable.

Begin by understanding what the person was trying to achieve. Add information, another perspective or a useful question, and state what needs to change. Telling someone they are wrong, blaming them for losing an opportunity, dismissing their work or describing them as repeatedly incapable shifts attention from improvement to self-defence.

items: Comparisons that undermine the person. A compliment such as “This is much better than your usual work” can dismiss earlier effort instead of recognising the present achievement.
Blame. “You lost that project because you were disorganised” assumes a conclusion and invites a defence. Examine the actual sequence and missing action.
Using the past to close down an option. One unsuccessful event or customer approach does not prove that another attempt cannot be useful.
Noticing only what is missing. Recognising a project win only by pointing to every opportunity still open makes progress invisible.
Questions that mainly criticise. “Why is this still wrong?” gives little direction about the change required.
Always and never. Turn a general accusation into a specific observation about a date, action or result.
Recognition followed immediately by criticism. Separate appreciation from a discussion about a missing record, pricing decision or overdue task.
Sarcasm. Humour about someone's repeated mistake or late arrival can embarrass them without solving the problem.

blocks.h: Notice how your message is received. If the person becomes defensive, check the evidence, your wording and their understanding. A defensive reaction does not prove the performance concern is wrong, but it may show that the conversation needs a different approach.

For example: “Thank you for updating the project on time. The next decision and its owner are still unclear. Can we work through what you know and what needs to be checked?” This recognises effort, identifies the gap and keeps the standard visible.

subs.title: Ten questions that open another possibility

items: What other possibilities do you see?
Can you explain your reasoning?
Could another approach work?
Are there other facts we need to consider?
What support would be useful now?
What leads you to see it that way?
What else is true about the situation?
Can you explain what you mean in more detail?
Where did that information come from?
What observations support your conclusion or concern?

blocks.h: Recognise the person's feelings while checking a claim. The purpose is to examine information and find a useful response, not to pretend an inaccurate statement is correct.

sections.title: Build trust and address difficult issues

intro.h: Expertise and care become less helpful when a manager cannot admit a limitation or raise an uncomfortable issue. The Need to be Perfect habit can hide mistakes; the Pleasing habit can leave expectations unspoken. Trust needs both openness and reliable action.

subs.title: Show that it is safe to learn

blocks.h: Keep promises, be consistent, show respect and provide support. Also acknowledge a relevant mistake, limitation or development need of your own. Explain what you learned or what you are doing to improve. This makes it easier for others to ask for help without pretending to know everything.

Openness should be relevant and appropriate. It does not require sharing private matters or every thought. Do not use a disclosed weakness to ridicule the person or discourage future honesty. Be clear about confidentiality you can genuinely maintain in your management role.

Look for practical signs of trust. People admit mistakes, ask managers or peers for help, name the skills they need, discuss unhelpful communication, address working relationships and raise concerns early. They can discuss fears, attitude or professional conduct without treating every conversation as a threat to their standing.
Trust develops through repeated experiences. A good meeting does not make up for unreliable or dismissive behaviour afterwards.

subs.title: Five ways to build trust through shared experience

blocks.h: Use a level of openness that fits the existing relationship. Participation in personal sharing should remain a choice.

items: Learn something about each other. Invite a relevant background experience, interest or personal story the person is comfortable sharing. The purpose is understanding and connection.

Share three work experiences. Each person prepares a funny experience, a successful experience and a particularly challenging or unusual one. Discuss what the experiences reveal about working together.

Exchange contribution and improvement feedback. Once sufficient trust exists, each colleague identifies one valuable contribution and one development area for the person receiving feedback. Give everyone a turn to receive and contribute.
Name one development need and organise support. Each person chooses a weakness they want to work on. Colleagues help find practical support without treating the admission as a personal failure.

Seek feedback on communication. Use a developmental communication profile or invite trusted colleagues to describe how your communication is received, including strengths and blind spots. Keep the focus on development, and allow honest feedback without retaliation.

blocks.h: Do not move directly from a first introduction to high-risk personal feedback. Maintain respectful daily behaviour after any exercise.

Support sometimes means sharing an observation the person may not want to hear. Explain your intention, name the benefit, check that this is a suitable time and ask whether they are ready to discuss it. Then address the actual issue directly.
For example: “I want to help you avoid the same difficulty at the next contractor meeting. Can I share something I noticed in how the discussion ended?”
A supportive opening does not excuse aggressive language. Nor does asking about readiness make a fixed work requirement optional. Clarify the requirement, listen to concerns and agree how to meet it.

subs.title: State the outcome you want for the person

blocks.h: Distinguish what you want for the person from what you want from them. A specific benefit can make the reason for a difficult conversation clearer: “I want you to have enough information to enter that project meeting with confidence.”
This approach can help when:

items: Performance needs to recover and the person wants to regain confidence, satisfaction or financial reward.
A new way of working is needed to provide better tools, support or clarity.
You want to reinforce continuing commitment to fulfilling work, customer value and appropriate management support.
Disappointing results have reduced motivation, including where market or project conditions are outside the person's control.
A person needs coaching to handle a difficult customer or situation more confidently.

blocks.h: Use a benefit the person actually values. Avoid a generous-sounding phrase that only disguises the manager's preferred outcome.
An unexplained change deserves a question, not a conclusion about someone's honesty. Six useful signals are:

items: A sudden change in performance.
A change in attitude, energy or approach to work.
Different behaviour towards colleagues or the manager.
Reluctance to do something previously handled without difficulty.
Newly missed commitments.
A repeated difference between stated intentions and actions, such as postponing an agreed coaching meeting.

blocks.h: Confirm the person's view of the relationship, describe the observation and offer a tentative interpretation: “We have postponed our last two conversations. I wonder whether there is another concern about meeting. Am I understanding that correctly?”

Possible concerns include a difficult previous management experience, feeling intimidated, worry about job security, concern about colleagues' opinions, reluctance to say no or uncertainty about the value of coaching. These are possibilities to explore, not motives to assign.
The person's explanation may be accurate and straightforward. Accept a credible answer and do not keep questioning solely to confirm your suspicion.

sections.title: Make coaching a daily leadership practice

intro.h: Good coaching keeps the person responsible for their work while making the manager's support dependable. Understand the gap, choose the appropriate help, listen carefully and check assumptions. Connect effort with a meaningful outcome. Recognise progress, address concerns honestly and finish with a clear action and review.

The balance matters. Support without accountability can leave the issue unchanged. Accountability without understanding can become pressure. Questions without needed instruction can create confusion. Expertise without room for the person's thinking can create dependence.

subs.title: What to do differently this week

items: Choose one habit to change. Notice where you tend to take over, talk too much, assume or avoid. Start with one observable behaviour; add more only when manageable.
Use a real work situation. Discuss a current project decision, customer conversation or development need. Ask the person what would make the conversation useful.
Practise the chosen behaviour. For example, pause before answering, check an assumption or ask for the person's options before offering your own.
Agree a concrete next action. Make the owner, support, completion date and evidence clear.
Review the effect. Ask what was useful, observe what changed and keep a short record of the learning. Repeat a helpful behaviour consistently rather than replacing it after one attempt.

intro.h: A sales leader helps the salesperson decide where growth should come from, choose where to invest time and develop the capability required. The coaching approach should reflect the commercial task. Protecting an established position, introducing a different proposition and opening a new customer relationship require different behaviours and evidence of progress.

blocks.h: Revenue is the sum of the quantity sold of each product multiplied by its net selling price. If quantities use a comparable unit, revenue can also be written as total volume multiplied by the weighted average net selling price.

Product mix describes which products make up those sales. It affects the average selling price, but it is not a separate multiplier. A more relevant mix can increase revenue at unchanged individual product prices, but higher revenue does not automatically mean higher profitability.

For coaching, ask where the salesperson can grow suitable volume and develop the agreed product mix. Treat price as a commercial boundary: discuss it within the salesperson's authority and the applicable pricing rules. Check product economics and the effort required with the appropriate commercial information.

Map each growth initiative against relationships and products or propositions. Agree the level to analyse before placing it: a defined account, customer group or market. Use that definition consistently throughout the plan.

An existing relationship means an established working relationship with the organisation or decision-making network being targeted. An additional contact within the same account is not automatically a new customer. A new product or proposition means an offer being introduced to the defined customer group; it may already exist in Rockfon's range. Record what is new so that different salespeople do not classify the same task differently.

blocks.h: Use the map to make choices. The four routes do not require equal time. Maintain necessary service and account protection while deciding where additional growth effort should go.

subs.title: Deepen business with existing relationships and products

blocks.h: The task is to identify suitable business that the relationship is not yet winning or retaining. Familiarity can hide gaps in project coverage, influence, applications or share of relevant business.

Ask: Which suitable projects are we missing? Who makes or influences those decisions? What business goes elsewhere, and why? What would earn us a larger role? Is the relationship broader than one familiar contact?

Coach the salesperson to map decision-makers, investigate missed opportunities and agree purposeful account actions. Look for better access, validated opportunities and stronger follow-through. Repeated visits without new understanding are not evidence of deeper penetration. If the account has little remaining potential, reconsider the investment rather than demanding more activity.

subs.title: Broaden the offer within existing relationships

blocks.h: The task is to establish a relevant additional product or proposition. The existing relationship creates access, but does not prove that the new offer fits the customer's needs.

Ask: What customer need would this address? Who values that benefit? Who else must be involved? What makes the salesperson hesitate to raise it? What evidence, demonstration or technical support would help the customer decide?

Coach discovery and the explanation of value. Provide product training where knowledge is missing, then rehearse the conversation. Review confirmed needs, access to the relevant decision-makers and agreed evaluation steps. Avoid replacing discovery with a longer presentation or assuming that a trusted contact can approve every new offer.

subs.title: Open new relationships with an established offer

blocks.h: The task is to earn access, establish relevance and qualify suitable business. A salesperson accustomed to responsive existing customers may need help initiating contact and handling uncertainty.

Ask: Why this target? What do we know that makes contact relevant? Which introduction or channel could work? What should the first conversation establish? What evidence would justify continuing or stopping?

Coach target selection, opening language, referral requests and the transition to a useful next conversation. Observe or rehearse the actual words when needed. Review response quality, access gained and qualified next steps alongside activity. High outreach volume to unsuitable targets should lead to a change in approach.

subs.title: Establish new relationships with a new offer

blocks.h: The task contains two uncertainties: whether access can be established and whether the offer fits the intended market or customer group. Early work should test the assumptions on which further investment depends.

Ask: Which assumption could make this approach fail? What must we learn first? Which customer conversations would test genuine demand? What technical or commercial conditions need confirmation? What evidence would justify the next investment?

Agree a limited initial effort, the support required and a review decision. Involve relevant technical, marketing or commercial colleagues. Review validated needs, access and feasible applications before expecting the same results as established business. Stop or reshape the initiative when evidence contradicts the original case.

subs.title: Change the coaching when the commercial task changes

blocks.h: Illustrative application with design products: a salesperson knows an account well but has not introduced a relevant design proposition. The leader checks whether the barrier is product knowledge, confidence or access to a different decision-maker. They rehearse discovery questions and agree a customer discussion to validate the need. The first useful progress point is a confirmed need and an agreed evaluation step, not just giving a presentation.

Illustrative application with healthcare: a salesperson is asked to develop a segment in which access is limited. The leader first helps define suitable targets, the decision-making network and requirements needing specialist confirmation. They agree how to gain initial access and what the first conversations must establish. Progress is judged through learning and qualified opportunities before treating an order forecast as credible. Whether this uses an existing or new offer is a separate decision on the map.

For each chosen route, agree the opportunity, evidence, next progress point, capability required, time investment and review date. State which lower-priority work will get less time. When a salesperson cannot explain that trade-off, the plan may exceed available capacity.

intro.h: Customer segmentation directs sales effort. An ABC classification should influence which accounts receive deliberate development, how relationships are maintained and where time is invested. A segment label without a decision about how to engage the account has little practical value.

subs.title: Explain the categories and the evidence

blocks.h: Use the market's agreed ABC criteria. Explain how current business, accessible future potential, strategic relevance, relationship position and effort affect classification. Apply the same definitions across territories and account owners.

Where the market has not yet defined how the categories change engagement, agree that before assessing individual salespeople. A working starting point is A for priority investment or protection, B for selective development with a specific opportunity, and C for efficient coverage and service. These descriptions do not replace approved local criteria or create fixed revenue thresholds.

Keep three judgements visible: the account's attractiveness, our position and ability to win suitable business, and the next action worth funding. A highly attractive account with weak access may need development. A current major account may need protection. A time-critical project may justify temporary additional attention without permanently changing the account's category.

head: Responsibility
Leader's contribution
rows: Trainer
Explain why segmentation exists, demonstrate the criteria and work through an example
Mentor
Share relevant experience about potential, access, service effort and common errors
Coach
Challenge assumptions and help the salesperson reach a better account judgement
Governor
Maintain consistent criteria, resolve exceptions and ensure classifications guide activity

blocks.h: Ask: What supports this classification? Are we using current revenue, potential or both? Is the potential available to Rockfon, or does it describe the customer's entire business? Which projects, applications and decision-makers support the estimate? What has changed? What information would change our decision?

Watch for familiarity being mistaken for value, unsupported potential being treated as fact, and difficult access being used as a reason to overlook a strategically relevant account. Record an important unknown as an assumption to test, with an owner and a date.

Illustrative application: a familiar customer receives frequent visits and is proposed as A, but has limited suitable future work. A less familiar target has credible projects aligned with the market priority. The leader compares evidence and the effort required. The existing customer may retain an appropriate service plan while development time moves to the target. If the target's potential is unverified, the next decision is to investigate it rather than assign unlimited investment.

Agree the purpose, stakeholder coverage, contact approach and resources for each priority account. Use project timing and customer needs to choose contact frequency. A high category does not justify visits without a useful purpose, and a lower category does not remove required service.

Use the agreed segmentation in account and activity reviews. Compare actual effort with the intended approach. If an account consistently requires more service than planned, address the service method, resource allocation or classification. Do not leave the mismatch hidden in the diary.

intro.h: A salesperson needs a visible plan for the coming two weeks. Important commitments beyond that horizon should be booked as soon as they are known. The second week may be less detailed, but it should already contain deliberate commercial commitments.

Without this habit, the first person to contact the salesperson decides how the day goes. Strategic targets lose attention, customer access is arranged too late, preparation and follow-up are squeezed, and travel becomes inefficient. Avoidable unfinished work can extend into personal time. An empty forward diary can also hide reluctance to initiate difficult conversations.
A full diary is not proof of professional planning. Look for purposeful work, realistic capacity and reliable follow-through.

items: Review customer promises, project dates, next actions and internal responsibilities.
Identify the priority accounts, growth routes and development actions that need attention.
Book purposeful customer contact early enough to obtain access. State the intended outcome.
Reserve time for proactive work, preparation and skill practice.
Include travel, follow-up, CRM updates and the full effort behind each commitment.
Leave capacity for foreseeable incoming work, using experience of the territory's demands.
Resolve conflicts by moving, shortening, delegating or declining work within the person's authority.
Check that the plan fits working hours and still supports the agreed priorities.

blocks.h: Use entries that identify work and purpose. Replace a vague entry such as account work with a task such as prepare questions for the healthcare discovery meeting. Use a task list for small actions that do not need a dedicated appointment, with due dates where appropriate.
Major project dates may need planning months ahead. Two weeks is the minimum to plan, not a limit on planning.

subs.title: Teach the habit and review its quality

blocks.h: When the habit is missing, work through one real fortnight together. Ask the salesperson to prepare a first proposal, then demonstrate how to include the complete workload and make trade-offs. Check customer access, preparation and realistic travel rather than simply filling gaps.

At the next review, examine what happened. If the plan was unrealistic, revise capacity assumptions. If it was displaced, investigate the requests and decisions. If difficult strategic work was repeatedly avoided, coach the skill or confidence behind that pattern. Reduce supervision as the salesperson becomes reliable.

The leader must examine their own behaviour. Last-minute internal requests, unnecessary meetings and repeated changes of priority can undermine a workable diary. Preserve reasonable freedom in how the salesperson organises the work while maintaining required standards.

intro.h: Reactive work responds to an incoming event, such as a customer request or an unexpected issue. Proactive work begins because the salesperson deliberately initiates it. Strategic work advances an agreed market or development priority.

These categories overlap. A planned visit can be proactive yet add little to the strategy. A response to an incoming project enquiry can be strategically valuable. Judge both the reason for the work and its contribution.

blocks.h: Translate each priority into the time needed for execution, preparation and follow-up. Reserve that time in the diary. Use the actual workload and the commercial task to set the amount. No single percentage suits every territory.

Illustrative planning choice: a salesperson opening new relationships protects two 90-minute outreach blocks and one 60-minute preparation block each week. These are example commitments, not a standard quota. The leader and salesperson also allow time for the resulting conversations and follow-up. The blocks should name the target group and intended work.

When urgent work displaces a block, decide whether it should be rescheduled, reduced or deliberately cancelled. Repeated displacement requires a change in priorities, workload or behaviour. Moving the same block every week without reviewing the cause is not protection.

Before accepting extra work, ask: Does it need action now? Is this the right person? What happens if it is done later? Which existing commitment would move? Check whether another colleague or channel can handle it more effectively.
Useful responses include:
I can complete this by Thursday. If it is needed today, we need to agree which existing commitment moves.
I can help with the customer decision. The technical question needs the appropriate specialist.
Before booking another visit, can we clarify what it needs to achieve?

The salesperson should escalate conflicting priorities they cannot resolve within their authority. Protecting strategic time does not permit ignoring required work or a genuinely urgent customer issue. The leader must make the final trade-off where necessary.

subs.title: Review the pattern and the result

blocks.h: Compare protected time planned with time actually used for the intended purpose. Discuss what displaced it and the progress it produced. If the work happened but produced little value, coach target quality, preparation or execution. If it did not happen, diagnose capacity, boundaries or avoidance before increasing the target.
Use reasonable estimates. Excessive time logging can become another burden. The purpose is to improve commercial decisions and dependable execution.

intro.h: AI can support preparation, practice, analysis and drafting. The goal is better work and more capacity for valuable sales activity. The salesperson remains responsible for what they use, record and communicate.

subs.title: Choose a real task and suitable support

blocks.h: Start with a recurring task where the intended improvement is clear. Suitable practice may include preparing discovery questions from approved material, rehearsing a first call, challenging account assumptions, drafting follow-up from verified notes or improving the clarity of a message.

First ask the salesperson to explain the task and what good work looks like. If they cannot judge a useful result, teach the underlying sales skill before expecting AI to improve it. Demonstrate the tool where technical familiarity is missing; coach judgement where the person can operate it but accepts weak output.

subs.title: Use a five step working routine

items: Define the outcome, audience and required format.
Choose an approved tool and information permitted for that use.
Give a clear brief with relevant context, constraints and source material. Ask the tool to name any missing information and assumptions.
Check the result for accuracy, relevance, tone, technical claims and proposed commitments. Verify important sources independently.
Adapt and apply the result, then review whether the completed workflow improved the work.

blocks.h: Confident language and a plausible source reference do not establish accuracy. AI-generated research does not prove that a project exists, a customer has a need or a product meets a requirement. Customer-facing claims about performance, suitability, certification or compliance require current approved technical information and specialist support where needed.

Use only information permitted for the tool and purpose. Access to an AI service does not by itself authorise entering customer, commercial or personal information. Use sanitised practice material when permissions are unclear. Do not let generated drafts become records of events that did not happen. Do not send messages or commit the business automatically: first complete the required review and get the necessary authority.

Choose one use case and define the quality standard before trying it. Have the salesperson create a first result, explain their review and improve it. Compare the final work with the normal approach, including verification and editing time. Apply it to further suitable tasks before expanding.

For example, use an approved product brief and a sanitised customer situation to prepare discovery questions. Reject questions that assume an unconfirmed problem or imply an unsupported product claim. Keep questions that help establish needs and a useful next step. Rehearse the conversation so that the salesperson can use the questions naturally.

Ask: Why did you use AI here? What did you verify, change or reject? What did it miss? Could you explain the final message without the tool? Did the completed process improve quality or save time? Where will the saved time go?

If useful time is saved, deliberately reallocate it to agreed work. Assess judgement and work quality rather than prompt counts. If tool or data rules prevent the use case, select an appropriate alternative instead of treating that constraint as resistance.

sections.title: Start with a clear working relationship

intro.h: Regular coaching becomes useful when both people understand its purpose, make time for it and know what each will contribute. The aim is a reliable way to build skills alongside the work of moving projects forward and serving customers.

Introduce coaching as a practical working relationship. Explain how it differs from a sales update, technical instruction or a formal performance discussion. Ask about the salesperson's previous experiences and preferred support. A meeting placed in the calendar without this explanation can feel like another reporting requirement.

Before beginning, check that the manager can listen, investigate a gap, give honest feedback and follow through. The salesperson needs a real development need, and the ability to take part and act on it. Address a missing skill or resource rather than interpreting every difficulty as reluctance.

items: Prepare and introduce the relationship. Explain the purpose and potential value for this individual. Discuss previous experiences, concerns, expectations and how they prefer to be supported.

Agree a goal and starting point. Identify a useful outcome, the current evidence and the capability or behaviour that could help. In a long project cycle, include progress the person can influence before an order is secured.
Agree mutual responsibilities. State what the manager will provide and what the salesperson will own. Clarify work requirements and how concerns or missed commitments will be raised.

Agree a practical meeting rhythm and preparation. Protect time, decide what good preparation looks like and agree when extra contact between meetings would help. The salesperson should identify an agenda and progress to discuss.

Make the first conversation useful. Establish what the person wants to achieve, listen to the facts and investigate the actual gap. Adjust your initial view when new information appears. Provide instruction where necessary.

Finish with action and support. Agree an observable task or outcome, an owner, a completion date, needed resources and a review. Ask what was useful and what the manager should change in their support.
Review evidence and continue learning. Examine what happened, recognise specific progress and investigate barriers. Agree the next action and adjust the support or timing to the actual need.

blocks.h: Keep development coaching distinct from a formal employment decision. If a conversation has a formal performance purpose, say so clearly and explain the expectations, support and review arrangements.

intro.h: Coaching cannot depend entirely on spare time after every other task is complete. Consider the manager's selling responsibilities, team size and other commitments before agreeing a schedule. If the workload makes reliable coaching impossible, address capacity and support rather than repeatedly cancelling meetings.
Four planning questions help:

items: How much time does effective work in this salesperson's role require?
What time and practice will the person's development realistically need?
What contact is needed to build a useful manager–salesperson relationship?
How much time would we reasonably spend building a relationship with an important customer, and what does that suggest about developing our people?

intro.h: A weekly individual conversation is a useful starting option; a meeting every two weeks may fit some team sizes and workloads better. Agree the rhythm with the person and fit it to the development need. Use the rhythm as a planning choice and review whether it provides reliable support.

Group discussions can support learning but do not replace individual attention. A new skill, immediate issue or improvement effort may require additional contact. Where the manager cannot provide suitable support, consider whether another appropriately experienced or trained coach could help. Do not wait for an annual review to raise a development need that is already visible.

sections.title: Seven conditions that make coaching workable

items: Regular individual attention. Keep a predictable meeting rhythm that both people can sustain.
Mutual commitment. Agree that both people will prepare, participate and follow through.
Clear accountability and measurable objectives. Define what progress would look like and how it will be reviewed.
Dependable support. Remain respectful and available for development, including when a result is disappointing.
Appropriate questions and practical help. Use questions, instruction, a documented method or resources, depending on the actual gap.
Work between meetings. Agree specific actions, tasks or results that allow learning to be applied in real situations.
A realistic review period. Allow enough time to assess improvement in the role and project cycle. Where a turnaround is needed, agree what both people will do and when progress will be evaluated.

intro.h: These are continuing conditions of the relationship. A well-run conversation cannot compensate for repeated cancellations, unclear requirements or support that never arrives.

Measures should help the person and manager understand what is changing. In project sales, activity and orders may be separated by a long period and influenced by several parties. Review relevant activity, its quality and what it tells you about the project—not only a total number of contacts.

intro.h: Choose measures that fit the actual role and market. Agree the baseline, intended improvement, evidence, support and review period. Do not convert every possible activity into a quota or import another salesperson's call and appointment numbers. Check whether a measure could improve while the underlying work remains unchanged.

sections.title: Begin coaching with the annual personal development plan

intro.h: The annual personal development plan connects market strategy with the salesperson's commercial priorities and capability development. Agreeing the goals and the approach is the first coaching conversation. The plan should guide decisions through the year, including accounts, activity, practice and the leader's support.

The leader brings market direction, role expectations and commercial evidence. The salesperson brings account knowledge, experience, ambitions and an initial proposal. Explain fixed business requirements clearly while giving the person a meaningful role in shaping execution and development.

blocks.h: Share market priorities early enough for the salesperson to prepare. Ask for a short assessment of the current position: results, relevant pipeline, segmentation, growth opportunities, product mix, working habits and capability needs. Identify what should continue and what should change.

The leader should review the same evidence and check available support. If market direction is still provisional, identify the assumptions and book a date to confirm the plan. Do not present an unsupported target as an agreed strategy.

Commercial priorities may concern target accounts or customer groups, relevant products or propositions, account penetration, relationship coverage or the quality of suitable opportunities. Capability priorities should explain what the salesperson must learn or do differently to deliver that focus.

Attending cold-calling training is a learning activity. Opening relevant conversations with the agreed target accounts is the capability it should support. Where appropriate, define both, with practice and evidence that the skill is used.
Keep the number of priorities manageable. For each priority:

items: Explain its connection to the market strategy and this territory.
Establish the starting point and the evidence behind the opportunity.
Agree the intended outcome, timing and progress indicators.
Identify the capability, working method or habit needed.
Choose actions, resources, protected time and the work that will reduce.
Record the leader's support, dependencies and review dates.

blocks.h: Include commercial results and evidence available before those results arrive. A contact count describes effort. A confirmed need and an agreed evaluation step describe progress. Use both where useful, without treating either as a guaranteed future order.

Illustrative example only: the market priority is to develop an approved design proposition with selected existing accounts. The following numbers show how a plan can be made specific; they are not Rockfon targets.

head: Plan element
Illustrative agreement
rows: Focus and starting point
Review eight selected existing accounts. No suitable opportunities for this proposition have yet been validated in those accounts.
Commercial progress sought
By the end of the second quarter, establish four qualified opportunities for evaluation. Do not count a meeting or presentation alone as a qualified opportunity.
Evidence required
Confirm a relevant need, the decision-making roles, an appropriate application and an agreed next evaluation step. Record timing and important uncertainties.
Capability
Improve discovery and explain the proposition accurately in the customer's context.
Work and support
Research the accounts, arrange relevant conversations and rehearse discovery. The leader observes or joins an agreed conversation and arranges technical support where needed.
Time and trade-off
Protect a weekly development block. Reduce low-purpose repeat visits while retaining required account service.
Review
Check initial learning after the first customer conversations and review the full priority quarterly. Agree an appropriate commercial outcome once qualification and timing support it.

blocks.h: If the initial work reveals little suitable demand, review the target selection and proposition. If demand is credible but the salesperson cannot run discovery conversations well, increase focused practice. If the work was not attempted, examine capacity and follow-through. Different evidence should produce different coaching.

At quarterly reviews, decide what to continue, adjust, complete or stop. Change a priority for an explicit reason, such as new evidence, a strategic decision or a capacity constraint. Keep a record of the decision and its effect on time and support.
The normal development plan is separate from a formal performance improvement process. Do not wait for the annual cycle to address a visible development need or a required performance standard.

sections.title: Run connected personal development and sales personal development wheels

intro.h: The personal development wheel sets priorities and builds the capability to deliver them. The sales development wheel turns them into account choices, pipeline progress and activity. Information must flow in both directions: commercial reviews reveal coaching needs, and development priorities shape commercial effort.
Market strategy leads to the personal development plan, account and growth choices, planned activity and evidence of progress. Review that evidence to update the approach and the support required.

blocks.h: Schedule quarterly reviews at the start of the year. The final quarterly development follow-up can include annual evaluation and next-year preparation, provided each receives enough attention. Urgent learning or a material change in strategy should be addressed when it arises.

subs.title: Give each meeting a distinct purpose

blocks.h: For every meeting, the salesperson prepares current evidence and a proposed next decision. The leader prepares questions, checks earlier support commitments and identifies where a management decision may be needed. Use the shared operational records. Do not recreate the same information in a separate recurring report.

Review the starting point and strategy. Agree priorities, evidence, time, support and review dates. Produce the development plan.
