What specific skill, judgement or habit needs attention?
Work through a real situation, practise or investigate the gap, and agree an action and review point.

blocks.h: Meetings may be scheduled together, but preserve the distinct questions and decisions. On a quarterly review date, combine relevant preparation rather than ask for the same account information twice. A lengthy pipeline update should not consume the time reserved for development.

Record decisions with an owner, date, expected evidence and support. At the next meeting, begin with relevant previous commitments. Use a separate coaching conversation when a skill needs more practice than the commercial review can fit in.

Before the quarterly account review, the salesperson checks every account, updates evidence and proposes classifications. Make sure no account is left out, including inactive or poorly understood accounts. Discuss changed circumstances, major decisions, uncertainties and exceptions in more depth than stable accounts.

For each account, confirm the segment and rationale, opportunity, relevant growth route, engagement approach and next action. Compare effort across the portfolio with the available capacity. If too many accounts are labelled priority, challenge the classifications or resource assumptions rather than approve a plan that cannot be executed.

The leader owns consistency across the market. Calibrate disputed or materially different judgements with other leaders using the same criteria. Revisit an account between quarterly reviews when significant evidence changes.

subs.title: Add support without another recurring wheel

blocks.h: Maintain a weekly personal planning routine for the rolling two-week diary. Add observation, joint customer work or rehearsal when there is a defined learning need. Use an existing market leadership forum to calibrate segmentation, review strategic alignment and resolve shared obstacles.

Add a recurring meeting only when it makes a necessary decision that existing forums cannot make. A review of a lost or successful opportunity can be useful after an important event without becoming another standing meeting.

sections.title: Prepare people before asking for change

intro.h: Changes in working methods affect how people plan their day, work with customers and judge whether they are doing a good job. Even a useful change can create uncertainty when its purpose, practical effect or expectations are unclear.

For a project-sales team, a change might involve a different follow-up routine, clearer project information, a new handover responsibility or regular coaching. The leader's task is to explain the need, understand the effect on people, make the requirement clear and help them take the next step.
Preparation does not mean removing every concern before acting. It means giving people a fair opportunity to understand the change and a practical way to work through it.

blocks.h: Before introducing a new coaching relationship or way of working, check that you have:

items: Spoken individually with the people affected, where appropriate to the change.
Asked how they prefer to be supported and understood their readiness to participate.
Learned about relevant experiences with previous managers or changes.
Clarified expectations, needs and improvements they would value.
Explained your management approach and any important differences from earlier practice.
Explained the knowledge or preparation that enables you to provide the proposed support.
Clarified how coaching differs from reporting, instruction and ordinary management decisions.
Explained a meaningful benefit and checked the person's understanding and response.
Discussed your intentions, goals and expectations for individuals and the team.
Understood enough about the team's work and culture to avoid imposing a change based only on assumptions.

blocks.h: Explain a shared change to the team, then make room for individual conversations about its effect. Ask about uncertainty or rumours directly. People may understand the same announcement differently depending on their role and previous experience.

intro.h: Commitment means understanding the change, seeing a reason to engage with it and taking responsibility for an agreed action. It develops through a clear and honest conversation rather than a persuasive speech alone.

Connect the work requirement with a benefit that matters to the person or a shared purpose. Invite their view of how to make the change workable. Listen to concerns as information: they may reveal a practical barrier, a misunderstanding or a genuine disagreement.

Be honest about choice. Say clearly when a process or responsibility is required. The person may still be able to shape the method, timing within agreed limits or support. A development opportunity that is optional should not be presented as compulsory. Seeking commitment does not mean disguising a decision or promising that everybody will agree.

subs.title: Eleven situations that need a commitment conversation

items: A requested relocation.
A new or changed incentive arrangement.
Conflict or a need to rebuild common ground.
A change in policy, procedure, pricing, compensation or role.
A new coaching or development arrangement.
Recruiting or introducing someone to a role.
An employee leaving and the effect on the remaining team.
A requested change in behaviour or activity.
A problem that has been left unaddressed.
Accountability for performance or administrative requirements.
A task or request that someone is reluctant to take on.

blocks.h: Use the conversation to build understanding and clarify action. Its purpose and the person's choices will differ between these situations.

subs.title: The Six Steps of a Change Conversation

items: Get connected. Understand the person's situation and show that you are ready to listen. A brief, relevant experience can help if it creates connection; it should not replace the discussion.
State the possibility. Describe the broader improvement the change could make possible. Invite the person to consider an outcome worth working towards, without presenting it as a guaranteed result.

Ask permission to discuss it. Check whether this is a suitable time and whether the person is ready for the conversation. If a requirement must be addressed, explain its urgency and agree an appropriate way to proceed.

State what you want for the person. Make the specific benefit clear. A broad possibility might be more reliable project coordination; the individual benefit might be fewer last-minute requests and clearer preparation for their next meeting.
Have the conversation. Explain the request, change or opportunity. Clarify the evidence, what is fixed, what the person can shape, their response and what support is needed.

Agree a clear conclusion. Confirm concerns, next actions, ownership, support, a completion date and the evidence to review. Ask how the action will be carried out, what previous experience can help, what could interfere and how progress should be assessed.

blocks.h: Use the sequence naturally. Keep connection, honest intent, a clear request and an understood next step. Do not make the conversation feel like a script with six steps.

items: Remain open to the response. Do not become so committed to your preferred answer that you stop hearing relevant information.
Focus on a meaningful benefit or shared purpose. Avoid using the conversation mainly to protect your image or obtain a personal advantage.
Be genuine and appropriately open. Share relevant experience without unsafe or unnecessary personal disclosure.
Describe the desired improvement. Discuss consequences where needed, while also explaining what useful progress could look like.
Develop possibilities together. Invite workable alternatives rather than assuming there is only one method.
Attend to timing and circumstances. Someone dealing with a major project setback may need a different moment or opening for the discussion.

blocks.h: A supportive conversation can reduce unnecessary resistance. It cannot guarantee agreement. Check what remains unresolved and respond to it rather than treating every concern as a failure of attitude.

intro.h: Working quickly and completing the whole task are different things. Efficiency concerns time and effort. Effectiveness concerns whether the work achieves the required purpose and quality. Good performance needs both.

In project sales, a high number of meetings or proposals is not enough if requirements remain unclear or the next decision is not understood. When you raise a quality concern, use a specific example. Find out what is missing before you draw a conclusion about the person.

Ask them to help design a practical routine. Decide which information needs checking, when the work will be completed, what resource or technical input is needed and how the next handover will be made. Discuss the cost of continuing the problem without using an unverified worst-case story to create fear.

Accountability includes the manager's behaviour. Follow through on support, review what was agreed and address repeated gaps. If a commitment may be missed, the person should raise the concern before the due date and discuss a revised action. If a consequence is appropriate, make it transparent and agree how a future lapse will be addressed. An agreement the employee owns is different from using threats as the usual way to motivate people.

A short preparation note helps a leader explain the change clearly without writing a speech. Record the facts, the expected benefit and the questions that need discussion. Update your view when the conversation brings new information.

head: Preparation field
Question to answer
rows: Change and evidence
What needs to change, and what observable facts support that need?
Individual effect
What experience, concern, workload or constraint might matter to this person?
Broader improvement and personal benefit
What could the change improve, and why could that matter to the individual?
Requirements and choice
What is required, what is optional and what can the person shape?
Readiness for the conversation
How will you establish understanding and check that the timing is suitable?
Action and follow-through
What support, owner, completion date and review evidence need agreement?

intro.h: The situations are illustrative examples for discussion or personal reflection. They are not records of actual Rockfon events or claims about company policy.

subs.title: Introducing a new way of working

blocks.h: Maria takes responsibility for a regional project-sales team and wants to introduce regular coaching and a clearer project follow-up routine. She is tempted to announce the meeting schedule and begin immediately.

Before doing so, she discusses the purpose with the team and speaks individually about existing routines, previous management experiences and support needs. She explains what will change, what will stay required and what people can help shape. She asks what might make the new routine useful or difficult.

What to examine: Which assumptions could Maria make about readiness? What should people understand before the first meeting? How would she know that a concern is about workload rather than unwillingness? The useful outcome is a clear introduction and practical agreements, not simply a full calendar.

subs.title: Improving quality without slowing the work unnecessarily

blocks.h: Lars is active with contractors and regularly prepares proposals. A recent handover leaves a product requirement and a project decision unclear, so colleagues need to ask for missing information before they can proceed.

The manager first checks the evidence with Lars and acknowledges the work completed. They distinguish the number of responses from the quality of the complete response. Lars proposes a brief requirements check and time to complete the handover information after each relevant contact. Technical questions are referred to the appropriate specialist rather than answered from memory.
Five questions help examine the cost:

items: What does activity without complete, usable information cost the project and the team?
What does rushing the handover cost Lars and the colleagues who must clarify it?
What could an unclear requirement or incorrect record mean for the customer and the people making the next decision?
What could a wrong recommendation mean for project coordination, rework or the commercial relationship?
What could happen if an unsuitable solution were accepted because a requirement was not checked?

blocks.h: Agree how the check will fit the workload and what evidence will show that the handover is usable. Confirm product suitability and technical requirements using the relevant project information and current technical guidance.

Tom agrees to complete a project follow-up record but misses the deadline. The manager checks that the request, required information and date were understood, then asks what prevented completion. Tom identifies competing work and a routine that leaves administration until the end of the week.

They consider protected calendar time, a simpler record, shared planning, an accountability partner and available organisational tools. Tom chooses a workable routine and agrees to raise a likely delay before a future due date. He also agrees to come back within two days with a proposal. It should say how the manager should raise a missed commitment and what a fair response would be. They still need to agree that response and review whether the routine works.

What to examine: Was the difficulty understanding, capability, capacity or follow-through? What does the manager need to change? How would both people know that the new routine helps? The aim is a clear, owned agreement rather than a promise made under pressure.

items: Which managers have helped you develop, and what did they do?
Who built trust and respect beyond discussing production numbers?
Which management relationship improved how you worked or how you experienced your career?
Which relationships remained valuable after a role or job changed, and why?

blocks.h: Use the answers to identify a behaviour you want people to experience from you during change.

intro.h: People can take responsibility for a change more effectively when its purpose, effect and expectations are clear. Listen to their experience, distinguish requirements from choices and connect the requested action to a meaningful benefit. Address quality with evidence, and make both the leader's support and the person's commitment visible.
Agreement in a conversation is only the beginning. Progress depends on what happens afterwards: the action taken, the support provided and the response when something does not work as expected.

subs.title: What to do differently this week

items: Choose one real change or working requirement that needs a clearer conversation.
Write down the evidence, individual effect, fixed requirements and choices before discussing it.
Hold the conversation, check understanding and agree one practical next action with an owner and date.
Review what happened. Recognise progress, address the remaining barrier and follow through on your own commitment.

sections.title: Make Rocksell useful to the salesperson

intro.h: Use Rocksell as the shared operational record for relevant customer, project and sales activity information. The leader should explain the required standard and demonstrate how it helps the salesperson prepare, prioritise, follow up and obtain support.

Management reporting is one use. The salesperson also needs a reliable working view of their own business. Benefits depend on a usable process and accurate information. They do not appear simply because a system is in place.

blocks.h: Use one real account and project. Before a customer conversation, find the relevant history, contacts, project position and commitments. Prepare a useful objective. Show how the appointment is associated with the account or project through the configured Outlook connection. After the conversation, record what changed and the next action. Show where that action appears in the working view used by the salesperson and leader.

Explain the agreed relationship between Rocksell and the project database: which information belongs where, who maintains it and how records are linked. Where a link is manual, demonstrate it. Check how duplicates and conflicting updates are resolved, so that the salesperson knows which record is the correct one.

Verify what the local Outlook setup actually tracks or synchronises. Explain any manual action, the handling of changes or cancellations and how to check whether an appointment was linked successfully. Follow the agreed scope for business and personal information. Do not promise that all calendar entries or updates appear automatically.

subs.title: Explain the benefits through practical decisions

head: Need
Intended benefit
Demonstration
rows: Prepare a conversation
Relevant account history, people and project context are available together
Prepare for an actual meeting using the shared record
Connect customer relationships and projects
Different organisations and decision-makers can be understood in the same opportunity
Follow the configured links between account, contact and project information
Plan and follow up
Appointments, commitments and sales context remain connected
Use the enabled Outlook workflow and show the remaining manual steps
Decide what needs attention
A personal view identifies meaningful work and gaps
Use the salesperson's dashboard to select the next action
Obtain help or hand over work
A colleague can understand the position without rebuilding it from private records
Use the record to make a real request for support or handover

blocks.h: Show only available, functioning capabilities. When a connection or view is missing, name the person who owns the problem and the temporary way of working. Do not make the salesperson responsible for a system function they cannot enable.

subs.title: Replace parallel records with a workable process

blocks.h: Ask the salesperson to demonstrate what their spreadsheet does: what decisions it supports, what reminders it holds and why it feels useful. Preserve necessary work when moving it into the shared process.

items: Identify the information and decisions the spreadsheet supports.
Demonstrate the equivalent workflow in Rocksell or the agreed connected system.
Resolve material gaps in access, fields, views, ownership or duplication.
Agree where the operational record must be maintained and when updates are due.
Move active information in a controlled way, checking accuracy and duplicates.
Use the shared record in meetings and retire the duplicate recurring report.

blocks.h: Excel can support appropriate analysis. Changes affecting ongoing sales work must return to the shared operational record. If the leader continues requesting a separate spreadsheet containing the same data, the leader is maintaining the duplication they want to remove.

subs.title: Give the salesperson a useful dashboard

blocks.h: Start with the questions the salesperson needs to answer: What needs attention? Which next actions or commitments are overdue? Which priority accounts need engagement? Which opportunities lack a credible next step? Does planned activity reflect the growth priorities?

Use the available data and features to provide that working view. Explain each measure's definition, source, refresh timing and limitations. A dashboard should prompt a decision or action. If the data is missing or stale, correct the record or workflow before drawing a performance conclusion.

subs.title: Agree adoption and check it in practice

blocks.h: Define the required information, update timing and responsibilities. An activity record should clarify purpose, relevant outcome, changed information and the next action. A visit count without useful context adds little value.

Ask the salesperson to complete the workflow independently and explain how they check that it worked. Review a small agreed sample of live records and use those records in the next commercial meeting. Check accuracy, usable next steps and the ability to retrieve information, rather than logins alone.

If use is weak, distinguish a skill gap, a system obstacle, duplicated work and persistent refusal to follow the process. Address the actual cause. Leaders should prepare from Rocksell, maintain their own relevant commitments and stop requesting information already available there.

intro.h: A leader should explain, listen, teach and provide reasonable support. A continuing failure to meet a clear work requirement also requires a management decision. Disagreement, questions or low enthusiasm do not, on their own, show unwillingness. Examine behaviour and evidence.

head: Evidence to check
Appropriate response
rows: The person cannot explain the requirement
Clarify it and ask them to describe the expected work in their own words
They understand but cannot perform the task
Demonstrate, practise and provide appropriate training or support
Workload, access or a system prevents execution
Resolve the barrier or explicitly reprioritise the workload
They challenge the approach
Hear the concern, test the evidence and explain the final decision
They understand, can perform the task, have practical access and repeatedly do not comply
Make accountability explicit and involve HR where formal action is required

blocks.h: Do not infer motive from one missed commitment. A person may also demonstrate a process in training but struggle to execute it reliably in the actual workload. Test that distinction before concluding that the issue is refusal.

Describe the specific gap and its effect. Summarise the support already provided and ask what remains unresolved. Confirm the required behaviour, the evidence that will show improvement and a review date. Record the person's explanation and the leader's commitments.
Illustrative wording:

We agreed that active project records would contain a current next action by the agreed review date. These records still do not. We have worked through the process and provided the agreed support. What is preventing it now? We need to confirm the required change, the support that remains necessary and how it will be reviewed.

Keep the conversation factual. Avoid labels such as bad attitude or not coachable. If the requirement remains legitimate after hearing the concern, state that it applies even when the person would prefer another approach.

subs.title: Move into the applicable formal process

blocks.h: If the gap persists, involve HR and use the applicable local procedure. State clearly when the process becomes formal. Document the requirement, evidence, support, reasonable improvement period and possible consequences. Explain which consequences are allowed in this case. These may include formal warnings and ultimately the ending of employment, where the applicable process permits. Consider relevant health, disability or other circumstances through the appropriate process.

At the review, examine evidence and decide. Progress may justify continued support or a reasoned extension; persistent non-compliance may require formal action. Follow company policy and local procedure. Dismissal must not be a predetermined outcome.

If the required behaviour is now reliable, acknowledge the improvement and return to normal follow-up. If progress is partial, identify what remains and why any additional period is justified. If a previously unknown barrier emerges, act on it and revise the plan openly. If the person continues to refuse a clear requirement despite practical support, do not restart the same informal coaching indefinitely.
Judge the individual case. Do not let strong commercial results automatically excuse persistent refusal to meet legitimate working standards. Do not use escalation to silence useful challenge.

intro.h: Preparation, useful questions and a short practice record help you coach consistently in everyday work. Choose what fits a specific conversation or development goal. Avoid creating paperwork without a clear use.

sections.title: Fifteen questions to turn discussion into action

intro.h: A conversation is useful when insight leads to an action the person understands and can carry out. These questions help explore the method, resources, choices and commitment needed. Choose a few that fit the real gap. Give instruction when the person has not yet learned a task.

items: How do you plan to achieve it?
Which ideas could help resolve the issue fully?
What do you need?
Why does it matter to you?
Which skill would help you prevent this recurring problem?
Which three actions could you take this week?
What other perspective could help?
How can I support you best?
How would you like the situation to be?
What useful change can you make?
Which habit, action or way of thinking needs to change?
Which quality or behaviour do you need to bring to this situation?
What could become possible if the change happened?
What would continuing the current approach cost?
If you had a possible answer, what might it be?

intro.h: A useful question helps someone understand a situation, make a decision or take responsibility for action. Choose questions that meet the person’s need, not questions just to finish a list. Ask one at a time, listen to the answer and adjust naturally.

In coaching, the salesperson should usually talk more than the manager. An approximate 80–20 balance is a helpful reminder, not a rule or a score. Training, advice and management decisions need a different balance. A short conversation may need only a few well-chosen questions.

Ask about personal aspirations, feelings or financial priorities only where it is relevant, and only if the person chooses to answer. Keep to the boundaries the person sets. Avoid wording that suggests guilt or a hidden motive, or that turns a development question into a judgement about personal worth.

blocks.h: Use these questions to clarify responsibility and turn an intention into a realistic commitment. Discuss the person’s contribution without implying that they control every project condition.

items: Where could you take more responsibility, and which of your strengths could help?
What have you committed to, and what does keeping that commitment require?
Which actions show that you are working towards the goal?
What part did you play in the situation, and what have you already taken responsibility for?
What is your responsibility here, and what response can you choose now?
Which difficulties keep returning?
Which existing commitments could affect this deadline or expectation?
How much time will the task need, and when can you realistically make that time available?

blocks.h: Use these questions to make improvement visible and identify behaviour worth repeating. Look for changes in action and understanding as well as the final commercial result.

items: What is working, and what did you do differently this week?
What are your three most useful achievements this week?
Are recurring problems becoming less frequent? What evidence shows that?
How do you feel about the progress, and which achievement matters most to you?
What has changed compared with a month ago?
Have you recognised the progress made over the last few months? What has developed?

blocks.h: Use these questions when a useful discussion needs to become specific work. Agree an action the person understands, can influence and will be able to review.

items: Which capability would you like to use soon that you cannot yet use confidently?
What is the most useful next action, and how will it address the issue?
Which three activities could you commit to this week to support the goal?
Which behaviour or way of thinking would help you produce the result?
What important change could you begin today?
What will you complete before we next meet?
What is the most useful change you could start this week?
What will you do immediately after this conversation?
Which commitment would give us clear evidence of progress at the next meeting?
Which action are you willing to take to achieve the outcome?
Which old habit, activity or way of thinking is no longer helping?

blocks.h: Use these questions when attention is fixed on shortcomings and useful strengths or progress are being overlooked. Let the person decide whether wider personal priorities are relevant to the discussion.

items: What is leaving you dissatisfied with the current situation?
What is going well in your work or life at the moment?
Which aspects of your work or life do you particularly value?
Which achievement or resource might you be taking for granted?
Are you giving setbacks more attention than achievements? What would a balanced view include?
What makes it difficult to recognise an achievement now?
Which three things do you most value in your work or career?
If you feel satisfied with where you are, what effort or achievement has made that possible?

subs.title: Letting go of a fixed answer

blocks.h: Use these questions when someone is holding tightly to one expectation, explanation or method. Keep the work requirement clear while exploring flexibility in the response.

items: What are you holding on to that might prevent a better outcome?
Which belief or expectation is making the situation harder to change?
What are you trying to control?
Are we treating this as a choice between only two options? Could another workable option include useful elements of both?
What could you change in your own response that is within your control?

blocks.h: Use these questions to understand how the person interprets an event and how that interpretation affects action. Test explanations against evidence rather than replacing one unsupported belief with another.

items: What would help you feel more confident, motivated, organised or effective in this situation?
How is this way of thinking helping, and what is it costing you?
What does that word or idea mean to you in practice?
Which way of looking at the issue would help you act more effectively?
How might a different interpretation change your response?
How would you approach the meeting if you focused on checking project fit rather than proving that you must win it?
Which assumptions support your current explanation? Is another explanation possible?
What evidence supports that conclusion or concern?
Would it help to spend time on the skills or thinking behind the results, as well as the goals themselves?
How could you describe the situation in a way that is both accurate and more useful?

blocks.h: Use these questions to extend capability without making an unrealistic demand. First establish what the person can already do comfortably, then agree a manageable challenge and support.

items: If you were able to handle this, how might you begin?
If you had a possible answer, what might it look like?
What would a major improvement in your effectiveness look like?
Which uncomfortable but useful action could help you move forward?
What would be easy this week, and what would stretch you beyond that?
Which action this week would show your commitment to the goal?

blocks.h: Use these questions when the person feels that no useful response is available. Distinguish real constraints from choices about preparation, support, priorities or how to respond.

items: How could you remind yourself of the choices you still have about your response?
Which parts of the stress can you influence, and which conditions need support or escalation?
Would you choose to continue with your current approach? Why?
Is this something you want, a work requirement or an expectation you have placed on yourself?
What is limiting the choice, and which earlier decisions contributed to the situation?
What change in thinking could make another action possible?
Which choice could you act on now?
What options are available?

blocks.h: Use these questions to examine actual wording, listening and how a message is received. A description of a real conversation is more useful than a general opinion about communication style.

items: How do you usually communicate in this situation? What do you actually say?
What responsibility can you take for how the message is understood?
How would you describe your communication style, and how might others describe it?
What could make your communication more useful? Which belief or method might need to change?
Who communicates clearly and constructively in a way you could learn from?
Which part of your own approach could be contributing to the difficulty?
Are you listening to understand, or mainly preparing to gain agreement or close the discussion?
How much room do you give the other person to contribute?
Have you reached a conclusion before hearing the full explanation? How could you check?

blocks.h: Use these questions near the end of a conversation to understand what the person gained. Check the value against their needs rather than assuming that a long or positive conversation was useful.

items: Which part of the discussion helped, and how?
What useful insight, option or next step did you gain?
How did the conversation meet what you needed today?
What seems possible now that did not seem possible before?
What are you most interested in trying?
What changed in your thinking during the conversation?
How do you feel about the situation now?

blocks.h: Use these questions when recognising a cost could help someone decide to change. Explore the effect on the person, customer, project or team without turning the conversation into a threat.

items: What does continuing with this approach cost you?
How well is the method working, and what cost do you notice?
What could follow from this behaviour, and who else could be affected?
Where are the current actions likely to lead?
How does that affect you or your work?
How long are you willing to continue with the current difficulty before changing something?

subs.title: Helping the person develop an answer

blocks.h: Use these questions when the person has enough understanding to explore a solution but is returning the decision to the manager. Provide missing instruction or information where it is genuinely needed.

items: If you were coaching yourself, what would you ask or suggest?
Which natural strength could you use more fully in your work?
What do you suggest?
When you hear your own explanation, what stands out?
How have you handled a similar situation before?
Which unanswered question would make the next step clearer?
How would you like me to support you with this issue?
Why does it matter to you?
What process would you create for identifying projects, qualifying opportunities, preparing meetings, following up or organising the work?
How might the customer experience your approach, and what would you need to ask them to check that interpretation?
Which approach could help create the customer response you are seeking?
If you were the coach, which change would you ask for?

blocks.h: Use these questions to make the value of a proposed change concrete. Explain any fixed requirement honestly, then explore the benefit and what the person can help shape.

items: What would solving this recurring problem make possible?
What could improve if the proposed change worked?
What would a satisfying working day look like for you?
Can you describe how the improved situation would work in practice?
If your important work and personal goals were achieved, what would be different and what would you be doing differently?
What useful new possibility could this change create?

blocks.h: Use these questions when energy or commitment has reduced. Understand the reason and reconnect the next action with something the person values.

items: Are you waiting for a person, opportunity or time before acting? What can you begin now?
Which important goal have you stopped working towards?
What motivates you to improve?
Which capability or opportunity have you left undeveloped?
Which work or personal priority have you repeatedly postponed?
What would make it possible to give that priority some attention now?

blocks.h: Use these questions to check what has changed in behaviour and results. Ask for a specific example, rather than accepting a general claim that things are better.

items: What changed in your thinking this week, and what effect did that have?
How would you handle this differently from a year ago?
Which area did you improve this week, and what progress did you observe?
Describe one occurrence: what did you do, what did you expect and what actually happened?
Which repeated actions are improving your relationships with customers or colleagues?
What did you accomplish today?
What would clear progress in identifying or developing new project opportunities look like?

blocks.h: Use these questions to distinguish a real concern from an untested prediction and find an action available now. The feeling is real even when the predicted event has not happened. Actual risks still need attention.

items: What are you afraid might happen? Is it happening now, or is it a prediction?
Which consequence are you trying to avoid?
Has that feared outcome happened before? What actually occurred?
What is the worst plausible outcome if the concern becomes real?
Which three concerns relate to you personally, which three to your career and which three to succeeding?
Which parts of the prediction are supported by evidence, and which are imagined?
How are you imagining the feared outcome, and how are you imagining the outcome you want?
What can you do in the present situation while preparing for a possible future risk?
What would you like to happen instead?
What might the concern be telling you, and how could you respond constructively?

blocks.h: Use these questions to connect the work with capabilities and interests the person can develop. Shared standards can be met through different individual strengths.

items: Which ability feels most natural to you?
What do you enjoy doing, and when did you last do it?
What do you do well with relatively little effort?
How would you describe a role that made better use of your strengths?
What would you do more of or differently?
Where do you feel most capable?
Which personal qualities have contributed to your progress so far?
What gives you energy and interest in the day ahead?
Which part of your work is most interesting, and which is most satisfying?

blocks.h: Use these questions to distinguish a goal the person values from an expectation they have accepted without examining it. Connect the goal with resources, action and a review point.

items: Where would you like to be in ten years, and what might help you move in that direction?
Which goal do you genuinely want to work towards over the next 60 days?
What motivates that goal, and what would you change now?
When would you like to achieve it, and what is your approach?
What do you want to avoid, and which future regret would you prefer to prevent?
Is this your goal, someone else’s expectation or a requirement of the role?
Which necessary resources are missing?

Choose one area and name three useful improvements. Areas include relationships, career, motivation, selling or professional skills, communication, work organisation, attitude, quality of life, financial priorities, or how others experience your work.

blocks.h: Use these questions only where financial goals are relevant to the development conversation. Let the person choose whether to discuss private financial circumstances; keep business expectations and personal worth separate.

items: What commercial or profit contribution is expected from the business or team?
Which financial goal matters to you, and what level of stability or reward are you seeking?
What is limiting progress towards that goal?
On a scale from one to ten, with ten the highest priority, how important is increasing earnings to you?
Which beliefs about money affect your decisions at work?
Which actions could materially improve your earnings or commercial contribution, and what would they depend on?
Which financial decisions or mistakes keep recurring?
Does your current reward reflect the contribution and responsibility you aim to provide?
Would a substantially higher level of responsibility and reward feel realistic to you? What makes you say that?

blocks.h: Use these questions before accepting more work. A clear response about capacity protects existing commitments and is more useful than agreement followed by a missed deadline.

items: How could you create more space for the work that matters most?
What does agreeing immediately cost when you have not checked capacity?
What does setting a boundary mean to you, and where did that belief come from?
Can you help others without repeatedly putting existing commitments at risk?
What would saying no to some requests make possible?
How do people you respect handle boundaries and decline requests?
Does this request need an immediate answer?

Which response fits best: thank the person and check your schedule before replying, consider the opportunity and agree a time to come back with an answer, or review existing commitments and come back with a realistic completion date?

blocks.h: Use these questions to let the person establish a useful focus. Combine a brief check-in with a clear purpose and relevant review of the previous commitment.

items: What do you need from today’s conversation, and what do you need from me?
How would you like me to support you? What should I do more or less of?
What is going well for you at the moment?
What would you like to leave with, and what would you like to learn?
What did you learn this week?
What did you do this week that supported your goals or the way you want to work?
How would you like to feel about the issue at the end?
Which one achievement would make this conversation worthwhile?
Which issue could we work on that would be particularly useful?
Before starting something new, can we review the action you agreed at the last meeting?
Which focus could help you make progress on several goals?

blocks.h: Use these questions when the current way of describing a situation leaves little room for action. Explore an alternative that can be tested, without promising that every constraint will disappear.

items: Which part of what matters to you could you begin now rather than postponing it for years?
What would a satisfying and successful year look like?
Which five business opportunities are you not yet using fully?
What could you do differently next time?
How would the choice change if you considered available opportunities as well as possible losses?
What other options are available, and what might you need to stop doing to make room for one?
What could become possible if the relevant change happened?
If the problem were resolved overnight, what would be different and what evidence would show it?
What new option could you create here?

subs.title: Understanding what keeps a habit in place

blocks.h: Use these questions when an unhelpful habit also appears to offer convenience, protection or a sense of control. Treat a possible benefit as something to explore, not as proof of a hidden motive.

items: What effort have you invested in continuing this pattern, and what does it provide for you?
What do you gain from the way you currently manage the work or your career?
Could continuing the activity, avoiding change or accountability, resisting a routine, complaining or blaming also help you avoid something uncomfortable? What might that be?

blocks.h: Use these questions when projects, requests, follow-up contacts and commitments compete for attention. Identify what would make the greatest useful difference, then protect time for it.

items: Why is this important, and what is most urgent?
Which problem currently feels hardest to resolve?
Which three changes matter most over the next 30 days?
Which three opportunities deserve attention over the next 30 days?
Which underlying problem, if addressed, would reduce several other difficulties?
Which activity this week would most support your goals and give a sense of progress?

blocks.h: Use these questions when the person reacts negatively or seems uncertain. Keep your impression tentative: the response may reflect a concern, missing information, a real constraint or disagreement with the proposal.

items: I may be hearing a concern about what I said. Have I understood that correctly, and what is behind it?
Do you feel we are considering the options openly, or is something making that difficult?
Would it be useful to hear another perspective?

intro.h: At the next review, record what happened to protected work and the commercial progress it produced. Use the same definitions across the periods being compared.

Protected time completion percentage equals time used for the intended protected work divided by time originally reserved, multiplied by 100. Strategic time share percentage equals time spent on agreed strategic activities divided by total working time reviewed, multiplied by 100.

If the planned time is zero, record “not applicable”, not zero performance. Show deliberate changes of priority. These measures show patterns. They do not measure the quality of work, and they do not justify detailed time surveillance.

Sales leaders in Rockfon manage three connected disciplines. Pipeline and Opportunity management directs the business we are trying to develop and win. Account management directs the relationships in which we invest. Visit and Activity management directs the work and time used to deliver those choices.

The sales development wheel connects these disciplines through regular decisions. An account priority should influence the diary. Customer activity should improve a relationship, clarify an opportunity or produce another useful outcome. What we learn should change the account approach, opportunity action or allocation of time.

blocks.h: Pipeline management examines the whole set of opportunities: creation, size, quality, mix, timing and movement. Opportunity management examines the evidence and actions needed to advance one piece of business. A pipeline can be large but weak, or small because new opportunities are not being generated. These situations need different responses.

Opportunity management focuses on a specific piece of potential business, the relevant decision and the person responsible for advancing it. Business may arrive early or late, through different contacts and routes. Record where it is now and what decision comes next. It does not need to pass through every earlier step to become valid.

Account management examines the organisation, the relationship and the business we could maintain or develop. It considers strategic fit, accessible potential, stakeholders, current business and the effort needed. Segmentation is a decision about investment and engagement, using the shared ABC definitions.

An account plan should identify a commercial focus, the people and relationships required, the growth approach, actions and support. Its purpose is to direct work. A list of contacts and historical sales is useful evidence, but is not an account plan on its own.

Visit and Activity management covers planned and completed customer work, including onsite visits, remote conversations, outreach, preparation and follow-up. It also examines how travel, internal commitments and incoming requests affect capacity.

The leader checks both professional execution and commercial relevance. Activity needs to happen, but a high count alone does not show that the right customers were engaged or that opportunities advanced. The review should improve choices, preparation and follow-through while maintaining clear accountability for agreed work.

intro.h: Use three individual meetings and one team meeting. The individual meetings examine the salesperson's territory, judgements and execution. The team meeting coordinates shared opportunity traffic, responsibilities and support. It should resolve matters that benefit from the team being together.

blocks.h: Why: maintain a relevant, credible pipeline and help the salesperson advance important opportunities. What: a review of the pipeline followed by coaching on two opportunities chosen beforehand. How: use the latest-created and largest-opportunity lists, diagnose the main pipeline gap, spot-check one record and run two must-win opportunity deep-dives.

Good looks like a clear decision about where effort goes next, with customer-facing actions, support and owners. Red flags include inflated values, unsupported dates, an empty pipeline disguised by a few large entries, or a meeting spent reading every record aloud.

Why: direct investment towards the right accounts and relationships. What: segmentation governance, portfolio choices and review of the plans for every A account and other agreed in-scope accounts. How: the salesperson prepares the complete portfolio first; the leader challenges classifications, checks stakeholder coverage and reviews account choices.

Good looks like credible classifications and practical account plans that change engagement. Red flags include segmentation completed during the meeting, familiar accounts receiving most attention without justification, and A accounts with weak stakeholder coverage or no clear focus.

Why: turn commercial priorities into purposeful work and a feasible diary. What: review completed activity, coverage, preparation, proactive commitments, reactive demand and routes. How: examine patterns and exceptions, spot-check a visit and inspect the next two weeks together.

Good looks like the right people being engaged, useful outcomes and protected time for agreed priorities. Red flags include a busy diary with little strategic work, repeated displacement of proactive blocks, large opportunities or A accounts outside their agreed coverage, and avoidable travel.

Why: coordinate incoming and moving business, remove cross-functional barriers and improve the approach to must-win opportunities. What: changes in the team pipeline, ownership and handovers, delivery timing, support decisions and selected deep dives. How: review traffic by exception and use the team's expertise on normally two preselected must-win opportunities.

Good looks like one shared position on responsibilities and specific commitments that help the opportunity owner act. Red flags include a round-robin replay of every individual review, double-counted opportunities, unclear handovers or collective discussion without an accountable owner.

blocks.h: The sales leader books the year ahead and invites specialists or colleagues only to the items requiring their contribution. These durations are protected minimum working time. Use more time when the scope needs it. If activity meetings are monthly, the salesperson still refreshes the rolling two-week diary weekly; do not leave weeks three and four without a planning routine.

Use the same definitions, preparation standards, decisions and scoring meanings across Rockfon. Market context may affect how evidence is interpreted and which action is appropriate. It does not create separate market definitions or criteria.

Opportunities can enter at different points. A specification may name Rockfon, name a competitor or be generic. Business may also first become visible late in the process, through an installer. Establish the current decision, our position and the next action from that starting point, using the shared definitions.

subs.title: Responsibilities for preparation and follow up

blocks.h: The salesperson prepares their commercial evidence and carries out their customer and planning actions. The sales leader acts as coach, prepares questions, confirms decisions and owns management support and follow-up. In team meetings, the opportunity owner takes on the salesperson's responsibilities for that opportunity. Named contributors own their agreed support actions. Each preparation and follow-up task below identifies its owner.

subs.title: Prepare decisions rather than extra presentations

blocks.h: Use the shared CRM records, dashboards, calendar and agreed sales data. The salesperson updates the relevant records by the previous working day, identifies important changes and brings a proposed action. The leader reviews the views beforehand and identifies questions and exceptions. Invite contributors early enough for them to prepare.

Correct straightforward data problems before the meeting. Where the data is still weak, mark the limitation, decide what can responsibly be concluded and assign the correction. Do not treat absent information as zero, and do not spend the full meeting entering records. If the data is too weak for a useful conversation, leave the meeting and ask the salesperson to use the time to update the records.

subs.title: Close every meeting with a manageable action list

blocks.h: Record the decision, the action, one accountable owner, the due date, expected evidence and required support. A customer-facing action should describe the progress we want with the customer, not just 'follow up'. A management action should name who will remove the barrier or make the decision.

The salesperson updates the source records. The sales leader emails the meeting notes from the cockpit straight after the meeting, and the salesperson replies with any corrections by the next working day. For a team meeting, the sales leader circulates the shared record and each opportunity owner updates their opportunity. Close an action when the evidence shows it is complete. Keep action completion separate from the commercial result. Review overdue or blocked actions at the next relevant meeting and act earlier where waiting would put business at risk.

Give each opportunity one accountable owner at a time, with other contributors named. Apply the shared handover rules, identify the person accepting ownership and confirm the next external action. The person who identified or influenced the opportunity may remain a contributor after ownership changes.

A specification milestone and a commercial sale are different outcomes. Record specification or influence progress separately from a secured Rockfon order and the timing of delivery or invoicing. Do not count the same opportunity again when a different role takes it over. Use one record or a clearly linked reference that produces one opportunity total.

Hold this meeting monthly for at least 90 minutes, with the salesperson and sales leader. The salesperson operates the relevant views and owns the commercial actions; the leader challenges evidence, coaches the approach and commits support. Invite another role or specialist for a selected opportunity when their input can change the next decision.

Use the Pipeline dashboard, the two pinned opportunities, the deep-dive in the cockpit and the notes from the previous meeting. The meeting should produce a diagnosis of pipeline health, priorities for creating or moving opportunities, a plan for each coached opportunity, and any quality corrections or support decisions.

subs.title: Read the pipeline indicators as a diagnosis

blocks.h: Creation: examine the count and known value of new records, their sources and qualification. Ask whether they represent genuinely new or newly discovered business and whether the sources are producing relevant opportunities.

Volume and coverage: examine the open opportunity count, known Rockfon value and concentration in a few large records. Compare with the role's objectives, historical conversion and lead times where these are genuinely comparable. Do not use one fixed pipeline multiple for every role, and do not treat specification influence value as an order-sales target.

Vertical mix: inspect hospital, office and other relevant market categories, including unknown. Ask whether the pipeline supports the strategy and whether the entry approach fits each segment. A strategic gap should lead to a target and generation plan, not only a request for a larger total.

Product mix: inspect tile-only, grid-only and tile-and-grid opportunities, using the shared product categories. Where line values are reliable, review the value mix too. Do not add tile area to grid length as if they were one volume measure.

Timing: examine expected delivery or commercial value by quarter on an agreed basis, separately from the next decision date. Ask what supports the timing, what moved and why. Where deliveries span several quarters, use a credible allocation or keep an unallocated amount. A first-delivery date does not put the whole opportunity value into that quarter.

Progression and conversion: examine meaningful advances, stalled records, lost business and slipped dates. The velocity tiles show which input moved most against last period: open opportunities, average value, win rate or cycle length. When you calculate conversion, compare like with like: similar roles and similar opportunity groups. A CRM edit or a stage change without new evidence is not progress.

subs.title: Adapt the conversation to the main constraint

blocks.h: If the pipeline is too thin, identify which customers, verticals or products need opportunity creation. Use external project databases where relevant, customer discussions, referrals, market intelligence and other legitimate sources. Agree a short target list, a reason for contact, a qualification question and protected time. A database listing becomes a lead to investigate, not automatically a qualified opportunity.

If there are too few suitable opportunities for two honest must-win opportunity deep-dives, use the reserved blocks to qualify real leads and design the generation approach. Record this exception and the evidence required by the next review; do not manufacture opportunities or quietly abandon creation work.

If the pipeline is sufficiently broad but not advancing, work on decision access, the proposition, stakeholder action, customer timing and specific risks. Requalify weak records or stop spending on them. A healthy total is not a reason to accept unsupported close or delivery dates.

For a specification-focused role, examine relevant influence milestones, specification position, decision-maker access, handover quality and later commercial visibility. For field sales, examine access to the current purchasing or installation decision, competitive position, channel coordination and the order or delivery path. For account-focused roles, examine the commercial initiatives and relationships relevant to their responsibilities. Apply the shared definitions and evidence questions to the role and current decision.

Choose a record from the agreed scope rather than letting the salesperson curate every example. Open the evidence behind a material claim: who confirmed the need, how the value was estimated, which decision is next and what justifies the date. Check that the current owner and other roles agree on responsibility.

Distinguish a single recording error from a repeated misunderstanding. Assign a wider sample or a practical correction when a pattern appears. A sample is a quality check, not proof that the whole pipeline is accurate. Avoid public fault-finding. Do not use a missing field in place of understanding the opportunity.

subs.title: What good looks like and red flags

blocks.h: Good: the salesperson can explain the main pipeline gap, why the two opportunities deserve effort and what evidence will improve the position. Opportunity actions describe external progress and the leader has clear support commitments. Mix, timing and role context affect the plan.
Red flags: repeated date pushing, unverified large values, every opportunity scored highly, a list of activity with no customer advance, or the same support request remaining unresolved.

sections.title: The Must-Win Opportunity Deep-dive (as part of 1:1 Pipeline and Opportunity management)

blocks.h: In the 1:1 Pipeline and Opportunity management, the deep-dive helps the opportunity owner choose the next move. Start with the current decision and the outcome the owner wants to achieve. Examine five dimensions: need or pain, the right solution, access to power, the decision process and momentum. Use the questions to test the position and plan actions, not just to complete a score.

head: Dimension
Evidence to examine
Questions that improve the next move
rows: Need or pain
A relevant need, desired benefit, problem or reason for choosing, confirmed by the relevant stakeholder
What matters to them? Who confirmed it? What happens if they do nothing or choose another offer? Is our stated need their priority?
Right solution
Appropriate fit with the known requirement at a competitive price, a clear proposition and the technical or commercial checks needed
Why would our offer fit? What remains unverified? Who needs to evaluate it? Are we assuming a requirement that has not been established?
Access to power
Understanding of the people who can approve, specify, influence, purchase or block the current decision, and a credible way to engage them
Whose decision is this now? Do we have direct access or a reliable route through another person? Whose support or objection is missing?
Decision process
The current criteria, steps, responsibilities, timing and route to purchase or the next role milestone
What happens next, in what order and through whom? What evidence supports the timing? Could another party or route change it?
Momentum
Recent meaningful external progress and a realistic next step with an owner and date
What changed outside our CRM? What is the other party doing next? Is the date agreed or only hoped for? What would reveal that the opportunity has stalled?

blocks.h: Need or pain includes positive goals such as design intent, convenience, technical requirements like fire, reliable supply or a suitable application. It does not require the salesperson to invent a crisis. Access to power means reaching the people who matter for the current decision. It does not mean every opportunity needs a meeting with the most senior executive.

subs.title: Use a simple scale from one to four

head: Score
Evidence position
How to apply it
rows: Unknown or unsupported
We do not know, or cannot support the claim. State the missing information openly.
Partly supported
We have an internal hypothesis, indirect indication or incomplete evidence. Identify what is assumed and who or what could confirm it.
Confirmed for the current decision
The relevant stakeholder or a reliable identified source has confirmed the position. Record the source, date and any limitation.
Tested through action
Current evidence has been demonstrated or acted on, and the relevant next step is supported. Record what happened, not just that the salesperson feels confident.

blocks.h: For need, a four could mean the customer's priority has been demonstrated through evaluation, resource commitment or a decision. For solution, it could mean the required evaluation has confirmed the fit. For access, it could mean meaningful engagement with the relevant decision roles. For process, it could mean the agreed process has been validated through an actual milestone. For momentum, it could mean an agreed step was completed and the next external commitment is in place. These are examples of evidence, not additional mandatory stages.

A higher score includes the evidence for the lower ones. A four needs credible confirmation as well as action. Outdated evidence must be rechecked when circumstances change. Label a supplier's statement about the customer's position as indirect evidence if the customer has not confirmed it.

subs.title: Choose the gap that matters for the next decision

blocks.h: Score each dimension where the opportunity is today, then read the verdict. Early discovery may contain unknowns. They become unacceptable when the team is about to commit resources, or make a firm commercial assumption that depends on them.

Do not average the five scores into a probability of winning or use a high total to hide a critical weakness. An opportunity with strong need, solution and access may still be blocked by an unknown decision process. Unknown is a score of one, not 'not applicable'. If a dimension is genuinely not applicable to the defined initiative, record the reason and have the leader confirm the exception.
For each material gap ask: Where are we now? What evidence is missing for the next decision? What will we do to obtain or change it? Who owns the action, and when will we review the result?

blocks.h: The owner proposes before the leader supplies the answer. The leader can teach, advise or involve a specialist where the gap requires it. Do not use questions to make the salesperson guess a technical answer they do not have.

Illustrative example: an installer asks for a late quotation on a competitor specification. The salesperson proposes strong solution and momentum scores because the quotation is ready. The review finds that we do not know whether substitution is accepted or who approves it. There is no agreed evaluation step. The next action is to establish the approval route and suitable evidence with the relevant parties. Sending another quotation does not close those gaps. The opportunity need not recreate earlier architectural work if the present decision can be understood directly.

If 45 minutes is not enough for the portfolio, extend the meeting or book a second review block within the quarter. Uploading or briefly showing a plan does not prove that it was reviewed. Every in-scope plan must receive the required review; reserve deeper time for material decisions and risks.

Salesperson: Check meaningful contacts and decision roles for every A account. Identify relationship gaps, single-contact dependence and unreliable contact details.
Salesperson: Review time and activity by segment, last engagement, known pipeline and actual business. Explain effort that differs from the agreed approach and flag due or overdue coverage.
Salesperson: Send proposed segment changes, the number of in-scope plans and decisions requiring coaching by the previous working day.
Sales leader (coach): Review the portfolio, proposed changes, exceptions and previous actions. Prepare challenges to assumptions and stakeholder coverage.
Sales leader (coach): Allocate enough time to review every in-scope plan. Extend the meeting or book an additional block within the quarter if the standard agenda is insufficient.

Has the complete portfolio been reviewed? What supports proposed changes? Are potential, strategic fit and our position being judged consistently? Check A-account data and stakeholder gaps.

subs.title: Start with segmentation governance every time

blocks.h: Confirm that the salesperson completed the portfolio review. Challenge the evidence behind changes and stable classifications where it is weak. Ask whether current revenue is being mistaken for future potential, whether the potential is accessible to Rockfon and whether familiarity is influencing the label.

Use the shared segmentation criteria. The leader governs consistency and confirms exceptions, but should hear the salesperson's knowledge before deciding. If the preparation is incomplete, record the gap and a completion date. Use the meeting for the decisions supported by evidence and arrange the missing review; do not count an incomplete portfolio as signed off.

Enough stakeholders means enough credible coverage of the account's relevant decisions, not an arbitrary number of names. Depending on the account, this may include commercial decision-makers, specifiers or technical evaluators, purchasing, operations and people influencing access or implementation. One person may hold several roles in a small account.

For every A account, ask: Who can grow, protect or block the relationship? Which roles are covered by meaningful access? Where are we dependent on one person? Who has changed role? Which relationship must be built next and why? A name in the CRM does not establish an active relationship.

subs.title: Review each account plan through five questions

items: What is the commercial focus for the next quarter and its connection to the market strategy?
What evidence supports the opportunity or protection need, including current business and accessible growth potential?
Which stakeholders, decision roles and relationship gaps affect that focus?
What is the growth or account approach, and which actions could change the position?
What effort, support, next milestone and review point are justified?

blocks.h: For a specifier or other influencing account, examine access to relevant decision roles and known influenced opportunities. Explain how those relationships connect to later commercial activity. Keep the account's influence distinct from sales invoiced to another account.

subs.title: Use the account indicators to reallocate effort

blocks.h: Start at segment level. Time by segment and activity type shows whether the engagement approach is being executed. Use recorded duration as a reasonable approximation and keep missing classifications visible. Examine whether high effort reflects valuable development, required service, inefficient work or familiarity.

Known pipeline and actual business show different parts of the account's contribution. Distinguish the account billed for sales from accounts influencing an opportunity. When one opportunity links to several stakeholder accounts, do not add each link to the portfolio total. That would count it more than once.

Last meaningful engagement and required coverage show where relationships are neglected or contact is poorly targeted. A useful call and an onsite visit may serve different purposes. Set and review the required visit or engagement period for the account rather than assuming that one logged interaction satisfies every requirement.

items: Sales leader (coach): Confirm segmentation decisions, reasons and any exception or review date.
Salesperson: Update segmentation and every reviewed account plan. Record the named owner and date for missing evidence and stakeholder actions.
Salesperson: Put engagement decisions into the activity plan and diary, including what will receive less effort when another account receives more.
Salesperson: Check the emailed meeting notes, reply with any corrections by the next working day and complete the agreed customer and relationship actions.
Sales leader (coach): Email the meeting notes from the cockpit straight after the meeting and arrange agreed introductions and support, with a named owner and date.

Sales leader (coach): Complete any additional review block within the quarter and confirm that every in-scope plan has been reviewed. Follow up material changes before the next quarterly meeting when necessary.

subs.title: What good looks like and red flags

blocks.h: Good: every account is accounted for, the required plans have been reviewed, classifications have reasons, and the salesperson can explain why effort differs across the portfolio. Priority accounts have a clear focus and meaningful stakeholder coverage or a plan to obtain it.

Red flags: all accounts become priorities; segment changes have no evidence; A accounts have no usable plan; contact names are mistaken for relationships; actual effort never changes after the review.

Hold this meeting every two weeks as the default, for at least 60 minutes, with the salesperson and sales leader. A monthly rhythm can be used where the planning habit, coverage and follow-through are reliable. Go back to meeting every two weeks when repeated gaps need closer support.

Use the Visits & activity dashboard, completed activity records, account and opportunity priorities, and the actual calendar for the next two weeks. The outcome is a realistic forward plan, corrected coverage gaps, better preparation and an agreed balance of proactive work and reactive capacity.

Explain the purpose directly: we need to understand whether agreed work happened, whether the right people were engaged and how time should be used next. Avoid implying that the salesperson's entire contribution is represented by recorded visits. Keep the review factual and proportionate.

items: Salesperson: Refresh completed activity, outcomes and next actions for the review period. Distinguish completed, cancelled, postponed and planned work.
Salesperson: Check activity classifications and account or opportunity context using the shared CRM requirements.
Salesperson: Review required coverage of A and other priority accounts, large opportunities, strategic target groups and important stakeholder roles. Flag due and overdue engagement or visits.

Salesperson: Prepare the next two weeks in the calendar, including customer commitments, proactive work, preparation, follow-up, records, travel and realistic reactive capacity. Add a location to each customer booking so the visit map can show the routes.
Salesperson: Review routes and time between appointments. Identify weak long-trip purposes and opportunities to combine relevant contact.
Salesperson: Prepare one example of reactive work displacing a priority, with a proposed response. Update the material by the previous working day.
Sales leader (coach): Review activity, coverage, the forward diary and previous actions. Prepare questions about priorities, execution and capacity.
Sales leader (coach): Select one completed visit or engagement for a random check and one upcoming activity for a preparation check.

What happened to agreed activity, calendar or preparation changes? What remains blocked?
5 to 15

Which activities produced useful outcomes? What incoming work took time? What did we deliberately change, miss or cancel, and why?

Are priority accounts, large opportunities, new target groups and relevant stakeholders receiving required attention within the agreed periods? Decide the gaps to close.
