subs.title: Review reactive work without dismissing its value

blocks.h: Field sales often responds to incoming requests and opportunities. Ask what the reactive work achieved and whether the salesperson was the right person to handle it. A timely response to an important customer issue can be commercially valuable.

Then examine what it displaced. Could the request have been handled through another colleague, a remote conversation, a different service channel or an agreed later time? Did genuine urgency require the change, or did every request receive an immediate yes? Did the leader create the interruption?

Classify how work began separately from what it contributed. Reactive and proactive describe initiation; strategic describes connection to agreed priorities. A strategic activity may be reactive, and a proactive visit may have little strategic value. Do not add these overlapping categories into a false total.

subs.title: Govern coverage of people and business

blocks.h: Use due lists based on agreed coverage periods, not one visit target for everyone. Every A account and large in-scope opportunity should have a required engagement approach, owner and next due date appropriate to its context. Include onsite visits where required; a phone call should not silently replace an agreed onsite purpose.
Check four types of coverage:

items: Priority accounts and required relationship maintenance or development.
Large opportunities and the people relevant to the current decision.
Strategic customer groups and new targets that would otherwise receive no incoming demand.
Relevant contacts and roles inside large accounts, including dependence on one relationship.

blocks.h: Ask: Which important account or opportunity is outside its period? Are we visiting the people we know rather than those who affect the decision? Is a large account receiving broad coverage or repeated visits to one person? What contact would produce a useful next step?

Coverage can involve different modes. Record onsite visits, remote meetings, calls and other activity separately. Do not count a delivery, sample drop or unanswered call as a completed, substantive conversation. Count it only if the shared definition and the actual outcome support that.

For the completed engagement, ask the salesperson to explain the situation without relying on the activity label. What was the objective? Why this person and this timing? What preparation was done? What did the other party say or decide? What changed? What is the next action?

For the upcoming activity, ask what the desired outcome is, what information or material is needed, who should attend and which questions will test the current assumptions. If the purpose is weak, improve or reconsider the activity before it consumes travel and customer time.

A useful record is concise but explains the outcome. A visit with no progress can still teach something valuable. Record what was learned and how it changes the approach. Repeated contact without new learning or a next move needs a different plan.

subs.title: Check the full two week capacity

blocks.h: Inspect the calendar together. Include the full workload behind customer appointments, not only the meeting itself. Check preparation, travel, follow-up, internal commitments and availability. Allow a realistic buffer for incoming work based on the territory's actual pattern.

Illustrative capacity calculation: a fortnight contains 80 working hours. Known commitments, including their travel, preparation and follow-up, use 52 hours. The remaining 28 hours split into 16 hours of extra planned strategic work and 12 hours of reactive capacity. These numbers illustrate a choice; they are not Rockfon standards. If actual incoming work repeatedly needs more capacity, change the allocation or service approach.

Do not allocate the same hour twice. Proactive blocks should name a task, target group and intended outcome. Reactive capacity is time available for incoming demands, not proof that those demands will occur. When a block is displaced, decide when to reschedule it or explicitly change the priority.

If the meeting is monthly, check the coming two weeks in detail. Confirm how the salesperson will update the following two weeks during weekly planning. Use calendar visibility for work planning within the agreed privacy and access arrangements.

Group suitable customer contact by geography and practical travel windows. Check the sequence, distance, travel time and time needed at the customer. Use the visit map in the dashboard, or a simple area or town view.

Before approving a long trip, ask: Why must this contact be onsite? Can other relevant visits be combined without creating low-value calls? Could a remote conversation achieve the objective? Does the route leave time to prepare and follow up? What happens if one appointment is cancelled?

A cross-country trip for a small number of contacts may be justified by business importance, access or a critical decision. Make the reason explicit. Do not chase visit counts or travel efficiency if this harms an important customer outcome. Do not add unnecessary visits just to justify the mileage.

items: Salesperson: Update the next two weeks in the calendar and maintain the agreed weekly planning routine.
Salesperson: Book or initiate contact for coverage gaps, with an intended outcome and due date.
Salesperson: Improve preparation for the sampled upcoming activity and record its outcome afterwards.
Salesperson: Record proactive commitments, reactive capacity and any rescheduled or deliberately cancelled priority work. Correct routes and unnecessary travel.
Salesperson: Check the emailed meeting notes, reply with any corrections by the next working day and complete the agreed activity and planning actions.
Sales leader (coach): Email the meeting notes from the cockpit straight after the meeting and arrange the agreed leader or specialist support.
Sales leader (coach): Deliver support commitments and review recurring capacity or execution problems at the next meeting. Check urgent coverage gaps earlier where needed.

subs.title: What good looks like and red flags

blocks.h: Good: the diary shows commercial choices and a feasible workload. Priority people and business receive timely attention, activity has a purpose and outcome, and proactive work is both protected and executed. The leader can explain why a lower count may be appropriate or why more targeted effort is required.

Red flags: a diary planned only day by day; every incoming request treated as urgent; activity concentrated on familiar contacts; no time for preparation or follow-up; repeated visit logs with no support; strategic blocks moved again and again; or impractical travel. An attractive dashboard with no reliable underlying activity is also a gap.

Hold this meeting monthly for at least 120 minutes. The sales leader chairs it with the relevant team. Include the specification, field and account roles relevant to the opportunities and decisions. Invite technical, marketing, supply or other colleagues for the items requiring their decisions or expertise.

Use the Pipeline dashboard with team scope, the opportunity table sorted by last updated, the owners’ deep-dive scores and the notes from the previous meeting. The purpose is to coordinate work and improve important opportunities. Individual development feedback that does not help the team belongs in the individual setting.

items: Opportunity owner: Update changes, ownership, contributors, next decisions, quarter expectations and support needs by the previous working day.
Opportunity owner: Flag new opportunities, meaningful progression, wins, losses, removals, timing slips and ownership gaps. Identify uncertainty explicitly.
Opportunity owner: Check shared records and possible duplicates, and flag disputed ownership to the sales leader before the meeting.
Sales leader (coach): Review team traffic and previous commitments. Resolve ownership questions that can be settled beforehand and prepare the decisions requiring the team.

Sales leader (coach): Select normally two must-win opportunities using business importance, strategy, timing, risk and need for shared support. Tell each owner the decision the deep dive should address.
Selected opportunity owner: Score the five deep-dive dimensions with evidence, and prepare a proposed next move and the specific help needed for the selected deep dive.
Sales leader (coach): Circulate the agenda and invite the contributors needed for the selected decisions.
All participants: Read the main changes and relevant deep-dive material before attending. Prepare any contribution requested; a separate pipeline presentation is unnecessary.

blocks.h: Traffic means the movement of business and responsibility through the team. Ask what changed and why it matters. Do not read every opportunity or ask every person for the same length of update.

For new business, decide whether it is relevant, who should qualify it and which role needs to act now. For progression, test the external evidence. For a slip, establish whether the customer timing changed, qualification was weak or our action was late. For a win or loss, identify a useful lesson or a consequential next action.
The team should understand the relationship between known pipeline, secured orders awaiting delivery and actual sales where these data are available. Keep them visibly separate.

At a handover, the outgoing and receiving people confirm the current position, relevant stakeholders, commitments, evidence, next decision and next external action. Record acceptance of ownership. A forwarded email or a changed owner field without this understanding is not a completed handover.

If two people need to act, distinguish the accountable opportunity owner from the owner of each specific action. Where ownership is disputed, the leader decides who acts now and resolves the wider rule outside the main discussion. Do not leave a live opportunity unattended while debating territory boundaries.

subs.title: Use team expertise in the deep dives

blocks.h: Use the same five-dimension scale as the individual meeting. Each 25-minute deep dive has five parts: three minutes to define the decision; five to test the deep-dive scores; ten to explore the main gap and options; five to decide actions and support; two to confirm the commitments.

Let the owner speak first. Ask contributors for information or a concrete action that changes the position. Separate a confirmed customer fact, an internal opinion and a proposed option. The leader prevents the room from becoming several people telling the owner how they would sell.

Must-win means priority attention and a deliberate plan. It does not allow unapproved pricing or unsupported promises. It also does not allow pursuing an opportunity after the evidence no longer supports it. The team can decide to requalify, reduce investment or stop.

items: Opportunity owner: Update the opportunity and next actions, confirm any accepted handover with the receiving owner and integrate agreed support into the next customer-facing move.
Sales leader (coach): Email the meeting notes from the cockpit to the team by the next working day, with accountable owners, dates and support commitments.
Named contributor: Complete the assigned support action by its due date and tell the opportunity owner the result or any barrier.
Sales leader (coach): Deliver their own support actions, check time-critical commitments before the next monthly meeting and remove cross-functional barriers.
Sales leader (coach): Carry relevant skill needs into individual coaching and recurring account or activity issues into the appropriate individual review.

subs.title: What good looks like and red flags

blocks.h: Good: the team understands incoming business, ownership and where shared effort is needed. Must-win discussions improve plans and secure support commitments. Team totals exclude duplicates and show uncertainty.

Red flags: everyone reporting in turn, unprepared deep dives, public blame, repeated handover gaps, unconfirmed commitments for absent colleagues, or discussion without decisions. Challenge any total that combines influence milestones, open potential, secured orders and invoiced sales.

sections.title: Simple dashboard build brief (DO NOT BUILD INTO THE PLAYBOOK YET)

subs.title: Build three working views and reuse the pipeline for the team

blocks.h: Provide one Pipeline and Opportunity dashboard, one Account dashboard and one Visit and Activity dashboard. The team meeting uses the pipeline dashboard with the appropriate team scope and a view of changes since the previous review. Do not build four separate reporting systems.

Start with readable lists, a few totals and links to the underlying records. Use existing CRM, sales reports and calendar views wherever possible. This brief specifies the information needed; it does not assume that a particular Rocksell feature or integration is already enabled. A useful saved view is sufficient where a new chart adds no decision value.

items: Show the owner or team scope, review period, market, currency and data refresh time clearly. Keep the selected scope visible when opening another view.
Filter by role, account segment, vertical and product category where relevant. Keep unknown classifications visible.
Let users open an opportunity, account or activity from the list. Show the responsible owner and the next action with its due date.
Keep actual sales, secured orders and open potential separate. Use the same agreed net-value basis when comparison is valid.
Respect the user's authorised scope and agreed calendar visibility. Distinguish missing access from absent activity.
If a metric cannot be supported, label it unavailable and show the underlying gap. Do not display a convincing zero or a fabricated trend.

blocks.h: Show a small header with open opportunity count, known open Rockfon value and the count with unknown value. Then provide these simple views:

What to show
Decision supported

Opportunities created since the previous review, newest first; owner, source, current position, known value, vertical, products and next step
Is enough relevant business entering, and who should qualify or act on it?
Largest and must-win
Open opportunities sorted by known Rockfon value, with must-win flags and unknown-value strategic opportunities visible
Where do concentration, risk or support require attention?
Quarter and mix
Credible expected value by quarter, unallocated value, vertical mix and tile-only, grid-only or tile-and-grid composition
Does timing and composition support the commercial priorities?
Exceptions and traffic
Overdue or absent next steps, stale evidence, timing slips, unowned records and material changes since the previous review
What needs correction, action, coordination or a handover?

blocks.h: Keep the two opportunities selected for individual coaching and the team must-win selections identifiable in these lists or through a saved filter. Make the five scores, evidence gaps and actions available for the coaching discussion.
For the team, show one opportunity total and the changes since the previous review: new, progressed, won, lost, removed and slipped.

Show the salesperson's complete portfolio, with a filter for A and other in-scope accounts. The main list should contain account, owner, segment, plan-review status, last meaningful engagement, next required contact or visit, stakeholder coverage gap, known associated pipeline and actual account business where available.

Add one compact view of recorded customer-activity time by segment and activity type for the selected period. Allow the leader to open the activities behind an account or segment. Keep unclassified and unlinked activity visible so that poor records do not create a misleading allocation.
Show a due list for missing plans, unreviewed classifications, stakeholder gaps and overdue required engagement. Use the shared definitions for segmentation, stakeholder coverage and engagement.
Use three simple views:

items: Completed activity for the review period, with type, account, contacts, purpose, outcome, recorded duration and next action. Link a known opportunity where relevant.

Coverage due, showing priority accounts, large in-scope opportunities, target groups or stakeholder roles needing contact within the agreed period. Show the last relevant engagement and the required next date or milestone.

The next two weeks of calendar activity, with location or area, purpose, proactive blocks, preparation, follow-up, travel and planned reactive capacity. Use the existing calendar alongside the dashboard if it cannot be shown directly.

blocks.h: Show planned proactive hours and the agreed reactive-capacity allowance. Review completion from recorded activity or an agreed reasonable estimate, rather than assume a calendar booking proves that the work happened. A simple town or area column is enough to discuss routes; automated route optimisation is not required.

intro.h: The development meetings maintain the agreed priorities and build the capability required to execute the sales development wheel. They should use evidence from account, pipeline and activity work. They do not repeat those reviews in full.

blocks.h: Starting format: 60 minutes with the salesperson and sales leader, extended when necessary. Hold it in time to guide the new planning year once market direction is sufficiently clear.
Before:

items: Sales leader (coach): Share market priorities and role expectations, review the previous plan and identify available support.
Salesperson: Review the previous plan and prepare current evidence and proposed commercial and capability priorities.

blocks.h: During: spend 10 minutes on learning from the current year, 10 on market direction and territory contribution, 20 on agreeing priorities and evidence, 10 on actions and support, and 10 on confirming time commitments and quarterly reviews. Define what the person should achieve and what they need to learn or do differently.
After:

items: Salesperson: Record the agreed development plan, including baselines, outcomes, actions, protected time and review dates. Carry the commercial choices into account, opportunity and activity work.

Sales leader (coach): Confirm the plan and support commitments, book the quarterly reviews and arrange the first coaching action. Where direction is provisional, confirm the assumptions and the date for resolving them.

blocks.h: Starting format: 30 minutes with the salesperson and sales leader. Book the four reviews at the beginning of the year. The final review can feed directly into annual evaluation and the next plan.
Before:

items: Salesperson: Update evidence against priorities, identify learning and obstacles, and propose adjustments.
Sales leader (coach): Review the evidence and progress on promised support before the meeting.

blocks.h: During: use five minutes for previous commitments, 10 for outcome and capability evidence, 10 for what should continue or change, and five for next actions and support. Ask what the salesperson can now do more effectively and how that is visible in the work.
After:

items: Salesperson: Update the plan and record the reasons for agreed changes. Complete the next development action.
Sales leader (coach): Confirm changes and support, arrange specific practice or coaching and check progress at the agreed date. Examine the result before removing a difficult priority.

blocks.h: Use a focused 30 to 60 minute conversation when the sales development wheel reveals a specific skill, judgement or habit to improve. Use five minutes to define the situation and outcome, ten to examine the gap, ten to practise or choose the approach, and five to agree how to apply it and review it.
Before:

items: Salesperson: Bring a real task or skill, the obstacle and the outcome needed.
Sales leader (coach): Review the situation and prepare the appropriate contribution: coaching, instruction, demonstration or specialist advice.

blocks.h: After:

items: Salesperson: Apply the agreed approach in actual work and bring evidence of the result to the review.
Sales leader (coach): Deliver agreed support and review the application at the agreed time.

blocks.h: Schedule this conversation as needed; it is not another compulsory standing meeting for every issue.

views.title: Expected Rockfon value per delivery quarter, by building segment
Expected Rockfon value per delivery quarter, by product type

intro.h: This chart is the question Rocksell has to answer: how much will we deliver, when, to which segments and in which product mix? If we cannot answer it with confidence, we cannot plan production, staff projects or steer the business. That is why we manage sales with structure.

items: Forecast
sqm
average price
win probability

blocks.h: Every opportunity carries these three numbers. Together they tell us how much will be delivered from each project, in which month or quarter, to which segment and in which product mix. Add them up across the team and you have the runway.
So we govern them. Not once a year in a budget, but every month, opportunity by opportunity.

subs.title: Govern the quality of the numbers

blocks.h: A forecast is only as good as the numbers inside it. Each one needs a question behind it.

items.title: Is the area right?
items.h: Too low and we under-plan. Too high and we over-promise.
ask: Is the sqm too low, or too high?
Are there other areas in the building we have not included?

items.title: Is the price right?
items.h: The price depends on which products we expect to win.
ask: Which price segment is the product in?
Does the price match the product mix we are proposing?

items.title: Is the probability earned?
items.h: Probability comes from evidence, not optimism.
ask: Has the opportunity passed the stage gate it claims?
What evidence supports the probability we have used?

subs.title: Govern that there is enough, and that it moves

blocks.h: Good numbers are not enough on their own. We also need enough of them, and they cannot sit still.

items.title: Number of opportunities
items.h: A healthy runway needs a steady flow of new opportunities in the right segments. When the count drops, the gap shows up in the forecast two or three quarters later.

items.title: Time spent on each deal
items.h: In our industry we are rarely in charge of a project’s speed. What we control is the time we invest in each deal and whether it still earns that time. Watch how long deals take, and where the hours go.

blocks.h: This is what the routines are for, in the 1:1s and in the team meetings alike. In the 1:1 Pipeline and Opportunity management, the leader and the salesperson test the numbers on each opportunity, and the Must-win opportunity deep-dive tests the evidence on must-win opportunities. In the Team Pipeline and Opportunity meeting, the whole team reads the runway together, sees what is moving and agrees where to act. The dashboards show it all on one page.
Structure is not bureaucracy. It is how we know what is coming, and how we make sure it arrives.

sections.title: What it means to be a sales leader at Rockfon

intro.h: Being a sales leader means taking responsibility for commercial performance and helping people build the capability to deliver it.

Your team needs direction, room to act and support when the work becomes difficult. The balance is autonomy with clear responsibility and accountability: people understand the priorities, make decisions within their role and follow through on their commitments.

We want to work in a more professional and structured way. That means clearer plans, purposeful customer engagement, reliable information and regular conversations about progress. These habits help people use their judgement well and make it easier to see where support is needed.
Your role is to create that environment: agree what matters, explain the expectations, coach the approach and address gaps with care and consistency.

sections.title: Expectations of sales leaders and sales reps

intro.h: Sales leaders provide clarity, coaching and follow-through.

items: Translate commercial strategy into clear priorities with each salesperson.
Agree what success looks like, what the salesperson owns and where decisions need support.
Prepare for reviews, ask thoughtful questions and help turn challenges into practical actions.
Make time for development, remove barriers and deliver the support you have promised.
Recognise progress and address missed commitments early, fairly and directly.

intro.h: Sales reps bring ownership, preparation and professional execution.

items: Build a plan that connects their accounts, opportunities and activities to the agreed priorities.
Maintain a forward diary, prepare for customer conversations and protect time for proactive work.
Keep CRM information current enough to support useful decisions and coordination.
Come to reviews with evidence, their own assessment and proposed next steps.
Follow through on commitments, raise risks early and ask for help when needed.

intro.h: Accountability works both ways. Reviews examine results, the quality of decisions and whether agreed actions happened. Where progress falls short, the conversation should find out what happened and what was within the person’s control. It should also look at what needs to change, including the support the leader gave.

Rockfon will keep changing. Markets move, customers change what they need, competitors change how they sell, and sometimes we simply want to do things better. Every one of those changes ends up at the frontline. Until the way our salespeople work changes, nothing has changed.

The easy response is to instruct, train or tell. Send the email, run the workshop, repeat it at the team meeting. It feels like action. It rarely changes what happens in front of a customer next Tuesday.

items: Cadence creates accountability.
Questions create ownership.

subs.title: Use the cadence to govern change

blocks.h: The meetings in this playbook are where change happens: one account, one opportunity and one visit at a time. Every change we want shows up in the work your team already brings to you. Use it, every time.

items.instead: Asking the team to be more proactive.
items.coach: Coach proactive work through their accounts and visits. Open the coverage list together and ask which customer they will contact before that customer calls them.

items.instead: Telling them to focus on Design and Mono.
items.coach: Look at the opportunity list together. Where Design or Mono fits, suggest presenting it as an option, or bringing a specialist to talk about it.

items.instead: Telling specification sales to make sure fire requirements are in the architect’s specification.
items.coach: While they present their pipeline, ask: “Is the fire requirement in the specification for this project?”

blocks.h: This is not policing. You are helping. The aim is that people contribute, and that they do it the right way, because they understand why it matters.

subs.title: Doing the right things, and doing them right

blocks.h: Your coaching covers both. Doing the right things is about choices: which accounts, which opportunities, which people and which products. Doing them right is about quality: the purpose, the preparation, the conversation in the room and the follow-up.
Instructions usually reach only the first. Most of the value sits in the second. Your role is to coach both, in every meeting.

items.title: Visits
items.h: The number of visits matters less than their quality. We register visits and talk about them to govern purpose and quality, not to count them. Ask what the visit was for, what changed and what happens next.

items.k: Done right, but the right thing?
items.title: A well-prepared presentation
items.h: A carefully prepared presentation to a contact who cannot influence the decision is done right, but it is not the right thing. Ask who decides, and whether this person can get us there.

blocks.h: Every meeting in your cadence is a chance to move the team a little further. Ask one more question than feels comfortable, and let them own the answer.

We built this playbook as a base to work from. It sets out a few fundamentals we agree on as sales leaders: a shared rhythm, common questions and practical tools. How you lead within it is up to you. Every leader has their own style, and this playbook is there to support it.

In it you will find what the role asks of you, the coaching skills behind good conversations, the sales management model and the routines of both wheels. Every meeting has its guide, instructions and a cockpit to run it live. The dashboards, the Must-Win Opportunity Deep-dive and the notes you send afterwards are there too. The toolbox holds the rest, for when you need it.
It will help you prepare faster, ask better questions and follow up on what was agreed. Above all, it will help you turn every meeting into a step forward for your team.
We hope you find it useful, and we wish you every success with your new way of working.

sections.title: What it will require from you

intro.h: This approach needs you to spend your time and attention more deliberately.
Consistency. Protect time for preparation, coaching and follow-up. Your team will judge how much these habits matter by what you do yourself.
Trust. Give people room to propose an approach, make decisions and learn. Agree when you will review progress and what evidence you will use.
Care and candour. Listen to the person’s circumstances and perspective. Be clear about a gap, its impact and the improvement needed. A difficult conversation can still be respectful and supportive.
Personal example. Bring the same preparation, reliability and openness that you expect from the team. Own your commitments and acknowledge when your own approach needs to change.
The aim is a team that can work more independently, because priorities are clear, plans can be trusted and people can rely on one another.
